title: 2  K-Nearest Neighbors
text:
2.1 Fitting a function without assuming its shape
Week 2, 9 September
Last week we distinguished four research goals. This week we begin working with prediction. We start with \(K\)-nearest neighbors because we can draw what it does. There is no probability theory or hidden optimization procedure to follow, and no coefficients to interpret. A picture lets us see how it produces predictions and where it runs into difficulty.
That visibility is useful while you are learning. Later in the block, the models will be harder to inspect. This first example gives us something concrete to compare them with.
Run the code as you work through the handout. We will assume it has run on your machine when we meet in the workshop.
We often ask how an outcome varies with another variable: how \(Y\) behaves conditional on \(X\), written \(P(Y=y \mid X=x)\).
One familiar approach is to assume a shape for the relationship and estimate its parameters. Ordinary least squares assumes a line; logit and probit assume particular shapes for binary outcomes. These are parametric models. Their usefulness depends partly on how well the assumed shape describes the relationship.
This approach gives us interpretable coefficients, standard errors, and a compact summary for a table. It also connects theoretical claims to quantities we can estimate. Much of the analysis in your other courses uses this framework.
The limitation is that more data will not fix an unsuitable shape. If the relationship curves, fitting a straight line to a thousand more observations still leaves us with a straight line.
We can respond by adapting the parametric model, perhaps through transformations, interactions, or logarithms. Alternatively, we can use a non-parametric method that makes fewer assumptions about the shape and lets the data play a larger role in determining it.
\(K\)-nearest neighbors is a simple example. Its prediction rule is:
There is no separate estimation step or set of fitted parameters in the usual sense. To make predictions, the model keeps and uses the data themselves.

title: 2  K-Nearest Neighbors
text: To predict the outcome for a case, find the \(k\) cases in your data most similar to it, and average their outcomes. If the outcome is a category rather than a number, take the majority vote instead of the average.

title: 2  K-Nearest Neighbors
section: 2.2 Drawing it: development and infant mortality
text:
2.2 Drawing it: development and infant mortality
Last week’s example concerned economic and political development. We established an association without settling its causal direction. We can set that causal question aside here, because prediction asks a different question.
Our dataset contains national development indicators for 199 countries and comes with the carData package.

install.packages(c("carData", "kknn", "caret", "scatterplot3d"))


library(carData)
library(kknn)

options(scipen = 999)   # print numbers in full rather than as 1e+05

data(UN, package = "carData")

countries <- na.omit(UN[, c("ppgdp", "infantMortality", "fertility",
                            "pctUrban", "lifeExpF", "group")])

# Express per capita GDP in thousands of dollars
countries$ppgdp <- countries$ppgdp / 1000

nrow(countries)

[1] 193

head(countries)

             ppgdp infantMortality fertility pctUrban lifeExpF  group
Afghanistan 0.4990         124.535     5.968       23    49.49  other
Albania     3.6772          16.561     1.525       53    80.40  other
Algeria     4.4730          21.458     2.142       67    75.00 africa
Angola      4.3219          96.191     5.135       59    53.17 africa
Argentina   9.1621          12.337     2.172       93    79.89  other
Armenia     3.0307          24.272     1.735       64    77.33  other


ppgdp records gross domestic product per capita, and infantMortality records deaths per thousand live births.
There are two small adjustments in this chunk. options(scipen = 999) makes R print numbers in full, such as 100000 rather than 1e+05. Dividing per capita GDP by a thousand keeps the axes readable. With this single predictor, changing the units cannot change which countries are nearest to one another, so it does not affect the model.
First, look at the data.

plot(countries$ppgdp, countries$infantMortality,
     col = "gray45", pch = 19, cex = 0.7,
     xlab = "Per capita GDP (thousands of US$)",
     ylab = "Infant mortality (per 1,000 live births)")








Infant mortality falls steeply among the poorest countries and then levels off. Compare the difference between countries at $500 and $2,000 with the difference between those at $30,000 and $40,000.
Now fit a straight line.

plot(countries$ppgdp, countries$infantMortality,
     col = "gray45", pch = 19, cex = 0.7,
     xlab = "Per capita GDP (thousands of US$)",
     ylab = "Infant mortality (per 1,000 live births)")

fit_ols <- lm(infantMortality ~ ppgdp, data = countries)
abline(fit_ols, col = "navy", lwd = 2.5)








The line misses the pattern systematically. It is too low for the poorest countries, too high in the middle, and eventually predicts negative infant mortality.
In a paper, we might address this within the parametric framework. Taking the logarithm of GDP per capita would straighten much of the curve. It also has a substantive interpretation: proportional differences in income may matter more than absolute differences.
Here we will use \(K\)-nearest neighbors, which does not require us to choose that shape in advance.

grid <- data.frame(ppgdp = sort(countries$ppgdp))

fit_15 <- kknn(infantMortality ~ ppgdp,
               train = countries, test = grid,
               k = 15, kernel = "rectangular")

plot(countries$ppgdp, countries$infantMortality,
     col = "gray45", pch = 19, cex = 0.7,
     xlab = "Per capita GDP (thousands of US$)",
     ylab = "Infant mortality (per 1,000 live births)",
     main = "k = 15")

lines(grid$ppgdp, fit_15$fitted.values, col = "maroon", lwd = 3)








kernel = "rectangular" gives all \(k\) neighbors equal weight. Other kernels give more weight to closer neighbors. We use the rectangular kernel because it matches the prediction rule described above.

2.2.1 What the algorithm actually did
For a country with GDP per capita of $2,000, the algorithm finds the fifteen countries closest to $2,000 and averages their infant mortality. At $3,000, it repeats the calculation with a slightly different set of neighbors.
The curve traces these moving averages. It depends on the observed neighbors rather than a separately estimated formula for the relationship.
This helps explain the wobbles where the data are sparse. There are few rich countries in the dataset, so their fifteen nearest neighbors may span a wide income range. The algorithm still produces a prediction, without warning us that the neighborhood may stretch across $40,000.

title: 2  K-Nearest Neighbors
text:
2.3 The choice of k
We chose fifteen neighbors without yet justifying that choice. Try several alternatives.

plot(countries$ppgdp, countries$infantMortality,
     col = "gray75", pch = 19, cex = 0.7,
     xlab = "Per capita GDP (thousands of US$)",
     ylab = "Infant mortality (per 1,000 live births)",
     main = "The same data, four values of k")

kvals  <- c(3, 15, 50, 150)
kcols  <- c("darkred", "maroon", "navy", "darkgreen")

for (i in seq_along(kvals)) {
  f <- kknn(infantMortality ~ ppgdp,
            train = countries, test = grid,
            k = kvals[i], kernel = "rectangular")
  lines(grid$ppgdp, f$fitted.values, col = kcols[i], lwd = 2.5)
}

legend("topright", legend = paste("k =", kvals),
       col = kcols, lwd = 2.5, box.lty = 0, cex = 0.8)








At \(k=3\), the curve follows local fluctuations closely. Some reflect the particular 199 countries in the dataset. At \(k=150\), the curve is almost flat: averaging so broadly removes much of the observed difference between rich and poor countries.
These examples show two different ways a model can perform poorly.
A small \(k\) follows small changes in the data. Some carry information about the relationship; others are noise. A model that reproduces the training data exactly also reproduces their noise, which need not recur in new cases.
We can express this by writing the outcome as
\[Y = \underbrace{f(X)}_{\text{signal}} + \underbrace{\varepsilon}_{\text{noise}}\]
We want to recover \(f\). The term \(\varepsilon\) includes measurement error, idiosyncrasy, and the particular histories of the countries observed here. Learning those details does not necessarily help us predict another sample.
The important distinction is between fitting the observations we already have and predicting new ones. A perfect fit to the training data does not establish that a model will predict well.
A large \(k\) has the opposite problem. It averages over countries that differ substantially and can smooth away a relationship we want to retain.

title: 2  K-Nearest Neighbors
section: 2.4 Why a perfect fit should worry you
text:
2.4 Why a perfect fit should worry you
To choose between these models, we need to evaluate them on observations excluded from fitting. We will split the data into a training set and a test set.

set.seed(7)

n        <- nrow(countries)
train_id <- sample(1:n, floor(0.7 * n))

Train <- countries[train_id, ]
Test  <- countries[-train_id, ]

nrow(Train)

[1] 135

nrow(Test)

[1] 58


set.seed() fixes the random draw, so you and I obtain the same split. Use it for random operations so that you can reproduce the analysis later and others can follow it.
For a continuous outcome, a common measure of prediction error is the root mean squared error:
\[\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[y_i - \hat{f}(x_i)\right]^2},\]
RMSE gives a sense of the size of prediction errors in the outcome’s units. Here those units are deaths per thousand live births. An RMSE of 15 means errors are typically around fifteen deaths per thousand.

rmse <- function(y, yhat) sqrt(mean((y - yhat)^2))

kseq     <- 2:60
err_test <- rep(NA, length(kseq))
err_train <- rep(NA, length(kseq))

for (i in seq_along(kseq)) {
  f_test <- kknn(infantMortality ~ ppgdp, Train, Test,
                 k = kseq[i], kernel = "rectangular")
  err_test[i] <- rmse(Test$infantMortality, f_test$fitted.values)

  f_train <- kknn(infantMortality ~ ppgdp, Train, Train,
                  k = kseq[i], kernel = "rectangular")
  err_train[i] <- rmse(Train$infantMortality, f_train$fitted.values)
}

plot(kseq, err_test, type = "l", col = "maroon", lwd = 2.5,
     ylim = range(c(err_test, err_train)),
     xlab = "k", ylab = "RMSE",
     main = "Error on data the model has seen, and data it has not")

lines(kseq, err_train, col = "navy", lwd = 2.5)

legend("bottomright", legend = c("Test (unseen)", "Training (seen)"),
       col = c("maroon", "navy"), lwd = 2.5, box.lty = 0, cex = 0.8)







kseq[which.min(err_test)]

[1] 17


Compare the training and test curves.
Training error falls as \(k\) gets smaller and is lowest on the left, where the model is most flexible. Choosing from training error alone would favor the most flexible model in this comparison.
Test error initially falls, reaches a minimum, and rises again. Beyond that minimum, the model is fitting details of the training countries that do not help with the test countries.
Before choosing \(k\), change the seed and rerun the code. The broad U shape remains, but the minimum moves. Avoid treating “the optimal \(k\) is 11” as a substantive finding about infant mortality: it depends on the split. We will use cross-validation to make the choice less dependent on one draw.

2.4.1 The same picture, drawn the conventional way
The horizontal axis makes this plot a little awkward. A large \(k\) gives a simpler model, so complexity increases toward the left. Textbooks usually draw complexity increasing to the right.
Plotting against \(\log(1/k)\) gives us that orientation, since it increases with model flexibility.

plot(log(1 / kseq), err_test, type = "l", col = "maroon", lwd = 2.5,
     ylim = range(c(err_test, err_train)),
     xlab = "Model complexity, log(1/k)", ylab = "RMSE",
     main = "Complexity increases to the right")

lines(log(1 / kseq), err_train, col = "navy", lwd = 2.5)

text(log(1 / 60), err_test[length(kseq)], "k = 60", pos = 4, cex = 0.8, col = "gray30")
text(log(1 / 2),  err_test[1],            "k = 2",  pos = 2, cex = 0.8, col = "gray30")

legend("top", legend = c("Test (unseen)", "Training (seen)"),
       col = c("maroon", "navy"), lwd = 2.5, box.lty = 0, cex = 0.8)








The numbers and conclusion are unchanged. We have simply redrawn them so that moving right means a more flexible model. This is the conventional picture: training error falls with complexity, while test error eventually turns upward.

title: 2  K-Nearest Neighbors
text:
2.5 Bias and variance
The terms bias and variance help us describe the two problems in this picture. You will encounter them throughout the statistical-learning literature.
Return to our earlier decomposition:
\[Y = \underbrace{f(X)}_{\text{signal}} + \underbrace{\varepsilon}_{\text{noise}}\]
There are two ways our estimate of \(f\) can go wrong.
Bias is systematic error. A model may be too rigid to capture the shape of \(f\), so additional observations do not resolve the problem. Our straight line through the infant mortality data is an example. So is \(K\)-nearest neighbors at \(k=150\), which smooths the curve into something almost horizontal.
Variance concerns how much the fitted model changes across samples. A model flexible enough to represent \(f\) may follow the observations so closely that another sample gives a noticeably different fit. The answer from one sample can then be unreliable even without systematic error in one direction.
Reducing one often increases the other. This trade-off helps explain the U-shaped test-error curve.



Test and training error as a function of model complexity. Reproduced from Hastie, T., Tibshirani, R., and Friedman, J., The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd edition, Springer, 2009.


This figure is a schematic rather than an analysis of a particular dataset. It illustrates the pattern we have just examined.
The arrows show the trade-off. Moving left gives simpler models, generally reducing variance but increasing bias. Moving right gives more flexible models, generally reducing bias but increasing variance. Training error falls throughout, so it does not help us locate the minimum of test error.

2.5.1 Seeing variance directly
With real data, separating bias from variance is difficult because we do not know the true \(f\). We cannot directly measure how far each fitted model is from \(f\).
Simulation lets us examine this. We choose a function, add noise, draw repeated samples, and fit a model to each. Since we know the function, we can compare every fit with it.

set.seed(1364)

N <- 1000
x <- rnorm(N, 2, 1)
f_true <- function(x) cospi(x)
y <- f_true(x) + rnorm(N, 0, 0.5)

sim   <- data.frame(x, y)
grid2 <- data.frame(x = sort(x))

kvec   <- c(5, 40, 150)
nsim   <- 30
ntrain <- 200
spot   <- 400                       # one x value we will watch closely
x_spot <- grid2$x[spot]

par(mfrow = c(2, 3))

preds <- matrix(NA, nsim, length(kvec))

for (j in seq_along(kvec)) {

  plot(x, y, col = "gray70", pch = 1, cex = 0.5,
       main = paste("k =", kvec[j]), font.main = 1)

  for (i in 1:nsim) {
    draw <- sim[sample(1:N, ntrain), ]
    f    <- kknn(y ~ x, draw, grid2, k = kvec[j], kernel = "rectangular")
    lines(grid2$x, f$fitted.values, col = "royalblue2", lwd = 0.4)
    preds[i, j] <- f$fitted.values[spot]
  }

  abline(v = x_spot, col = "gray40", lty = 2)
}

for (j in seq_along(kvec)) {
  boxplot(preds[, j], ylim = range(preds), col = "gray90",
          main = paste("Predictions at one point, k =", kvec[j]),
          font.main = 1, cex.main = 0.9)
  abline(h = f_true(x_spot), col = "red", lwd = 2)
}








These plots use thirty samples and three values of \(k\), all drawn from the same underlying function. The red line in the lower row marks the true value at the point being examined.
At \(k=5\), the fitted curves vary widely across samples. Their predictions are centered roughly on the true value, so bias is small, but an individual prediction may be far away. This is high variance.
At \(k=150\), the curves are very similar across samples. The estimates are stable, but the box lies far from the red line: they are consistently missing the true value. This is high bias.
At \(k=40\), the predictions are both reasonably concentrated and close to the true value, giving a better balance in this example.
Keep this in mind when reading a fitted model. A high-variance model may look convincing on the data used to fit it, without showing how much the result would change in another sample.

title: 2  K-Nearest Neighbors
text:
2.6 Cross-validation
Our choice of \(k\) depended on a single training/test split and moved when we changed the seed. There are two limitations to that approach:

The choice depends on which observations happen to be in each set.
We exclude thirty percent of the countries from training. With only 199 cases, that is a substantial amount of information.

Cross-validation addresses these limitations by rotating which observations are held out.

2.6.1 Leave-one-out
Leave one observation out, train on the remaining \(n-1\), predict the omitted case, and record its error. Repeat this \(n\) times, then combine the errors.
\[\text{RMSE}_{\text{LOO}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i - \hat{y}_i\right)^2}\]
Each case is used for testing once and for training in all the other fits. This removes dependence on one arbitrary split, but requires fitting the model \(n\) times.


2.6.2 k-fold
In k-fold cross-validation, we hold out groups rather than individual observations. Divide the data randomly into roughly equal folds. Train on all but the first fold and evaluate on that fold, then repeat with each of the others. Combine the errors after every fold has been used for testing.









\[\text{CV RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{\text{nfold}}\sum_{f=1}^{\text{nfold}} \text{MSE}_f}\]
Watch the two uses of the letter \(k\). The number in “\(k\)-fold” is unrelated to the \(k\) in “\(K\)-nearest neighbors.” We will use one to choose the other, so the code calls the fold count nfold to keep them apart.

cv_knn <- function(data, kvals, nfold = 10, seed = 7) {

  set.seed(seed)
  fold <- sample(rep(1:nfold, length.out = nrow(data)))
  out  <- rep(NA, length(kvals))

  for (j in seq_along(kvals)) {

    fold_mse <- rep(NA, nfold)

    for (f in 1:nfold) {
      tr  <- data[fold != f, ]
      te  <- data[fold == f, ]
      fit <- kknn(infantMortality ~ ppgdp, tr, te,
                  k = kvals[j], kernel = "rectangular")
      fold_mse[f] <- mean((te$infantMortality - fit$fitted.values)^2)
    }

    out[j] <- sqrt(mean(fold_mse))
  }

  out
}

You do not need to write this loop from scratch. You should be able to read it and explain what it does. That is the general expectation for code in this course.

kseq2  <- 2:60

cv_5  <- cv_knn(countries, kseq2, nfold = 5)
cv_10 <- cv_knn(countries, kseq2, nfold = 10)

plot(kseq2, cv_10, type = "l", col = "maroon", lwd = 2.5,
     ylim = range(c(cv_5, cv_10)),
     xlab = "k", ylab = "Cross-validated RMSE",
     main = "Choosing k by cross-validation")

lines(kseq2, cv_5, col = "navyblue", lwd = 2.5)

abline(v = kseq2[which.min(cv_10)], lty = 2, col = "maroon")

legend("topleft", legend = c("10-fold", "5-fold"),
       col = c("maroon", "navyblue"), lwd = 2.5, box.lty = 0, cex = 0.8)







kseq2[which.min(cv_5)]

[1] 24

kseq2[which.min(cv_10)]

[1] 27


Compared with the single-split curve, this one is smoother because each point combines errors from several held-out sets. The two fold counts also give broadly similar results.
Cross-validation does not identify a uniquely correct \(k\). Several values may perform similarly, and the exact minimum of a flat curve can reflect noise. Report the range of plausible choices, the value you selected, and your reason for selecting it.


2.6.3 The same thing, with caret
In practice, a package can handle this loop. Now that we have worked through cross-validation, we will use caret to implement it.
caret provides a common R interface for fitting and comparing predictive models. Install it now; we will use it again in Week 6.

install.packages("caret")


library(caret)

set.seed(7)

cv_caret <- train(
  infantMortality ~ ppgdp,
  data       = countries,
  method     = "knn",
  preProcess = c("range"),
  trControl  = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10),
  tuneGrid   = data.frame(k = kseq2)
)

cv_caret$bestTune

    k
26 27

plot(cv_caret)








Four arguments correspond to the steps we carried out by hand.
method = "knn" selects the algorithm. caret supports well over a hundred methods. Next week, we will change this argument to fit a random forest.
trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10) specifies cross-validation. number is the fold count, which we called nfold. Setting method = "LOOCV" requests leave-one-out cross-validation instead.
tuneGrid = data.frame(k = kseq2) supplies the values of \(k\) to compare. Without it, caret tries three values of its own choosing, which may not cover the range we want.
preProcess = c("range") rescales features to lie between zero and one, using the first of the two formulas from the previous section. You must request this explicitly; otherwise caret uses the raw units.
With one predictor, this rescaling does not change which countries are nearest to one another. We include it because scaling becomes important once we add a second feature, and it is useful to establish the habit now.
The result should be close to the loop’s choice, though caret draws its own folds. If the choices differ by a few units of \(k\) on a flat curve, that need not indicate a substantive disagreement.
Week 6 extends evaluation to rare outcomes, where accuracy can be misleading and we need other metrics.

title: 2  K-Nearest Neighbors
section: 2.7 More than one feature, and the problem of units
text:
2.7 More than one feature, and the problem of units
With multiple features, similarity needs a definition of distance. A common choice is Euclidean distance. For a case \(f\) with features \((x_{f1}, \dots, x_{fp})\) and a training case \(i\), it is
\[d_{if} = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{p}\left(x_{fj} - x_{ij}\right)^2}.\]
This extends straight-line distance to more than two dimensions. It also makes the units of our features important.
GDP per capita ranges from well under one to about a hundred, measured in thousands of dollars. Percent urban ranges from zero to a hundred, fertility from about one to seven, and female life expectancy from the high forties to the high eighties.

summary(countries[, c("ppgdp", "pctUrban", "fertility", "lifeExpF")])

     ppgdp             pctUrban       fertility        lifeExpF    
 Min.   :  0.1148   Min.   : 11.0   Min.   :1.134   Min.   :48.11  
 1st Qu.:  1.2398   1st Qu.: 39.0   1st Qu.:1.750   1st Qu.:65.10  
 Median :  4.4958   Median : 59.0   Median :2.264   Median :75.57  
 Mean   : 12.2911   Mean   : 57.1   Mean   :2.780   Mean   :72.08  
 3rd Qu.: 14.4973   3rd Qu.: 75.0   3rd Qu.:3.700   3rd Qu.:79.07  
 Max.   :105.0954   Max.   :100.0   Max.   :6.925   Max.   :87.12  


Using these raw units gives the wide-ranging features much more influence on distance. An income difference of fifty contributes two and a half thousand to the sum under the square root. The full fertility range contributes only about thirty-five. Features measured on smaller scales have very little influence, even if they are substantively relevant.
We can put features on a common scale using either of these transformations:
\[\tilde{x} = \frac{x - \min(x)}{\max(x) - \min(x)} \qquad \text{or} \qquad \tilde{x} = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{\sigma_x}.\]

rescale <- function(x) (x - min(x)) / (max(x) - min(x))

feats <- c("ppgdp", "pctUrban", "fertility", "lifeExpF")

countries_s <- countries
countries_s[feats] <- lapply(countries_s[feats], rescale)

summary(countries_s[, feats])

 1st Qu.:0.01072   1st Qu.:0.3146   1st Qu.:0.1064   1st Qu.:0.4355  
 Median :0.04173   Median :0.5393   Median :0.1951   Median :0.7039  
 Mean   :0.11599   Mean   :0.5180   Mean   :0.2843   Mean   :0.6144  
 3rd Qu.:0.13700   3rd Qu.:0.7191   3rd Qu.:0.4431   3rd Qu.:0.7936  
 Max.   :1.00000   Max.   :1.0000   Max.   :1.0000   Max.   :1.0000  


First, compare each feature with the outcome before and after rescaling. The transformation preserves that relationship.

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

plot(countries$ppgdp, countries$infantMortality, col = "maroon", cex = 0.7,
     xlab = "Per capita GDP (thousands of US$)", ylab = "Infant mortality",
     main = "Raw units", font.main = 1)
plot(countries_s$ppgdp, countries_s$infantMortality, col = "maroon", cex = 0.7,
     xlab = "Per capita GDP (rescaled 0 to 1)", ylab = "Infant mortality",
     main = "Rescaled", font.main = 1)

plot(countries$pctUrban, countries$infantMortality, col = "maroon", cex = 0.7,
     xlab = "Percent urban", ylab = "Infant mortality",
     main = "Raw units", font.main = 1)

plot(countries_s$pctUrban, countries_s$infantMortality, col = "maroon", cex = 0.7,
     xlab = "Percent urban (rescaled 0 to 1)", ylab = "Infant mortality",
     main = "Rescaled", font.main = 1)








The shapes of the point clouds are unchanged. Only the horizontal-axis numbers differ.
The change that matters for the model concerns the joint feature space, which these separate plots do not show.

2.7.1 What the algorithm now sees
With two features, countries sit in a plane rather than on a line, and we can plot the outcome above that plane.

library(scatterplot3d)

scatterplot3d(countries_s$ppgdp, countries_s$pctUrban, countries_s$infantMortality,
              color = "maroon", pch = 1, cex.symbols = 0.7,
              xlab = "Per capita GDP (rescaled)",
              ylab = "Percent urban (rescaled)",
              zlab = "Infant mortality")








Adding a third feature makes this picture harder to draw, because the outcome would require another dimension. The distance formula still works with any number of features. For more complex models, we will need to reason about spaces we cannot visualize directly.


2.7.2 What the neighborhood looks like
Choose a country and compare the twenty-five neighbors selected using raw units with those selected after rescaling.

target_raw <- c(median(countries$ppgdp),   median(countries$fertility))
target_s   <- c(median(countries_s$ppgdp), median(countries_s$fertility))

# Euclidean distance, exactly the formula above, computed by hand
dist_raw <- sqrt((countries$ppgdp     - target_raw[1])^2 +
                 (countries$fertility - target_raw[2])^2)

dist_s   <- sqrt((countries_s$ppgdp     - target_s[1])^2 +
                 (countries_s$fertility - target_s[2])^2)

nb_raw <- order(dist_raw)[1:25]
nb_s   <- order(dist_s)[1:25]

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

plot(countries$ppgdp, countries$fertility, col = "gray55", pch = 19, cex = 0.7,
     xlab = "Per capita GDP (thousands of US$)", ylab = "Fertility (births per woman)",
     main = "Raw units, k = 25", font.main = 1)
points(countries$ppgdp[nb_raw], countries$fertility[nb_raw], col = "red", cex = 1.6)
points(target_raw[1], target_raw[2], col = "red", pch = 19, cex = 1.7)
abline(v = target_raw[1], h = target_raw[2], col = "darkgreen", lty = 2)

plot(countries_s$ppgdp, countries_s$fertility, col = "gray55", pch = 19, cex = 0.7,
     xlab = "Per capita GDP (rescaled)", ylab = "Fertility (rescaled)",
     main = "Rescaled, k = 25", font.main = 1)
points(countries_s$ppgdp[nb_s], countries_s$fertility[nb_s], col = "red", cex = 1.6)
points(target_s[1], target_s[2], col = "red", pch = 19, cex = 1.7)
abline(v = target_s[1], h = target_s[2], col = "darkgreen", lty = 2)








The filled red point is our target country. The circled points are the twenty-five countries selected as its neighbors.
On the right, the rescaled features produce a roughly disc-shaped neighborhood. Both features contribute to the selection.
On the left, the neighbors form a narrow vertical band. They have incomes close to the target’s but span much of the fertility range. Income ranges over about a hundred units while fertility ranges over about six, so a small income difference can outweigh a large fertility difference. The units give income most of the influence without any explicit judgment that fertility matters less.
Both models return predictions without warnings. We could report the raw-unit version as a two-feature model even though one feature contributes very little. To notice that, we need to inspect the neighborhood.
This matters beyond the calculation. The model’s definition of similarity depends on which features we include and how we scale them. Leaving the raw units in place gives income much more influence. That is a consequence of our setup, even if we never explicitly intended to define similarity that way.

title: 2  K-Nearest Neighbors
section: 2.8 What this model cannot tell you
text:
2.8 What this model cannot tell you
There are no coefficients or standard errors to summarize this model, and no statement such as “a one-unit increase in \(X\) is associated with a change in \(Y\).” Its predictions depend on the data it retains.
The model also does not explain why richer countries have lower infant mortality. It uses the association between income and mortality to predict, as we discussed last week. Predicting well does not turn that association into an explanation.
Another limitation appeared in the neighborhood plots. The model returns predictions in the same format whether a case has many close neighbors or lies at the edge of the data. For the richest country, the neighbors may span tens of thousands of dollars in income. The output alone does not distinguish that prediction from one based on twenty-five closely comparable countries.

title: 2  K-Nearest Neighbors
text:
2.9 The politics of similarity
The model applies a simple rule: cases similar to past cases receive outcomes based on those past cases.
This resembles precedent in law, case-based administrative reasoning, and the Weberian ideal of treating similar cases alike. Consistency can support predictable, accountable administration, regardless of who handles a case.
With a fitted model, we should ask who defines similarity and how visible that definition is. In \(K\)-nearest neighbors, feature selection and rescaling determine it. These early technical decisions may receive little documentation or attention once a system is running, even though they shape its treatment of cases.
The model also reproduces patterns in the cases it was given. If those cases record unjust treatment, the model can carry that treatment forward while appearing consistent. This can happen even when the system operates as designed.

2.12 Questions for the session
Prepare an answer to at least two questions. We will use them to begin the session.

\(K\)-nearest neighbors has no coefficients and makes no claim about mechanism. Is it therefore useless for political science, or is that the wrong test to apply to it? Last week’s reading is relevant here.
The choice of \(k\) has no correct answer that can be read off the data alone. What does it mean that a central decision in a model is made by the researcher rather than discovered?
We rescaled the features so that income would not dominate the distance calculation. Suppose someone had not. Would you describe the resulting model as wrong, or as encoding a particular view of what makes two countries similar? Does the distinction matter for how such a system should be reviewed?
In the neighborhood figures, the left-hand model was given two features and used essentially one. It returned predictions and printed no warning. What follows for how a system you did not build should be reviewed before anyone relies on its outputs?
The model returns a prediction for the richest country in the data, assembled from neighbors that are nothing like it, and reports it exactly as it reports any other. Where in political or administrative use would that distinction matter most, and what would a responsible system do instead?
Bureaucratic rule-following and nearest-neighbor prediction both treat like cases alike. Identify one political difference between them that is not simply that the model is more complicated.

title: 3  Trees and Random Forests
text:
3.1 What trees are good at, and what they are not
Week 3, 16 September
Last week, we could trace each \(K\)-nearest neighbors prediction to a set of countries on a scatterplot. We begin this week with another model we can draw and explain: a decision tree. We then move to random forests, which trade some of that transparency for better predictive performance.
This comparison raises a question we will return to throughout the course. A model we can inspect is easier to explain and audit, but strong predictive performance often comes from models that are harder to interpret. Trees and forests let us examine this trade-off within one family of methods.
Statistical trees resemble the decision trees you may already know. Before fitting one, it helps to understand their main strengths and limitations.
Benefits.
This last point differs from \(K\)-nearest neighbors. Last week we rescaled features so that income would not dominate fertility in the distance calculation. A tree asks about one variable at a time, on its own scale, instead of calculating distances across features. Multiplying a feature by a thousand therefore changes the numerical split values but does not create the same scaling problem.
The main limitation is that a single tree often predicts poorly out of sample.
We will examine that limitation, then see how combining trees into a forest can help.

title: 3  Trees and Random Forests
text:
They capture interactions and non-linear associations without requiring us to specify those patterns in advance.
They can handle categorical variables, and individual trees are interpretable.
They are relatively fast compared with many other machine-learning algorithms.
They do not require the features to be rescaled.

title: 3  Trees and Random Forests
text:
3.2 Two datasets this week
Part I uses last week’s country data. Applying a new method to familiar data makes it easier to see how the methods differ.
Part II uses Fearon and Laitin’s civil war data (Fearon and Laitin 2003). The binary outcome is rare, which introduces a different set of problems.

install.packages(c("carData", "rpart", "rpart.plot", "tree",
                   "randomForest", "caret", "ggplot2"))


library(carData)
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
library(tree)
library(randomForest)
library(caret)
library(ggplot2)

options(scipen = 999)

data(UN, package = "carData")

countries <- na.omit(UN[, c("ppgdp", "infantMortality", "fertility",
                            "pctUrban", "lifeExpF", "group")])

countries$ppgdp <- countries$ppgdp / 1000   # thousands, as last week

nrow(countries)

[1] 193


This dataset has one row per country. Keep that structure in mind when we move to Part II.

title: 3  Trees and Random Forests
text:
3.3 Part I. A regression tree
Last week, we used \(K\)-nearest neighbors to fit the relationship between GDP per capita and infant mortality. Mortality falls steeply among the poorest countries and then levels off, so a straight line described it poorly. \(K\)-nearest neighbors followed the curvature by averaging over a moving set of neighbors.
A tree handles the same pattern differently. Comparing the two helps explain its prediction rule.

3.3.1 One feature

m_tree <- rpart(infantMortality ~ ppgdp, data = countries)

rpart.plot(m_tree, box.palette = "GnBu")








Each interior node has a rule such as \(x > c\). Follow the appropriate branch until you reach a terminal node, or leaf. Its prediction is the average infant mortality of the countries in that leaf.
Try reading one path aloud. You can describe the income ranges and predicted mortality in ordinary language, which makes this model relatively easy to communicate.
Now plot the tree’s predictions as a function.

oo  <- order(countries$ppgdp)
ddf <- countries[oo, ]

plot(ddf$ppgdp, ddf$infantMortality,
     col = "gray55", pch = 19, cex = 0.7,
     xlab = "Per capita GDP (thousands of US$)",
     ylab = "Infant mortality (per 1,000 live births)")

lines(ddf$ppgdp, predict(m_tree, ddf), col = "maroon", lwd = 3)

for (i in m_tree$splits[, 4]) {
  abline(v = i, col = "orange", lty = 2)
}








The leaves divide the predictor space into separate regions. With one feature, these are intervals marked by the dashed lines. Each interval receives the average outcome of its countries, producing the red step function. This is \(\hat{f}\): for a new country, find its interval and read the prediction.
The boundaries are close together on the left, where mortality changes quickly, and farther apart on the right. The algorithm chose these locations from the data without being told to space them this way.


3.3.2 The same data, two algorithms
Put last week’s model on the same plot to compare the predictions directly.

library(kknn)

grid <- data.frame(ppgdp = sort(countries$ppgdp))

knn_fit <- kknn(infantMortality ~ ppgdp, train = countries, test = grid,
                k = 10, kernel = "rectangular")

plot(ddf$ppgdp, ddf$infantMortality,
     col = "gray75", pch = 19, cex = 0.7,
     xlab = "Per capita GDP (thousands of US$)",
     ylab = "Infant mortality (per 1,000 live births)",
     main = "Tree and KNN on the same data")

lines(grid$ppgdp, knn_fit$fitted.values, col = "navy", lwd = 2.5)
lines(ddf$ppgdp, predict(m_tree, ddf),  col = "maroon", lwd = 3)

legend("topright", legend = c("Regression tree", "KNN, k = 10"),
       col = c("maroon", "navy"), lwd = c(3, 2.5), box.lty = 0, cex = 0.85)








Both methods produce step functions from local averages without assuming the relationship’s shape. They differ in how they choose which countries to average.
\(K\)-nearest neighbors uses a moving window with a fixed count. Here every prediction averages ten countries, regardless of whether their incomes are close or spread across forty thousand dollars. The sparse data on the right therefore produce less comparable neighborhoods and a less stable curve.
The tree chooses boundaries first and averages within the resulting regions. These can be narrow where the outcome changes quickly and broad where it changes slowly. Its steps are coarser, but their widths depend on the splits selected from the data.


3.3.3 What the algorithm is minimizing
We divide the feature space \(X = \{x_1, x_2, \dots, x_k\}\) into smaller boxes. After choosing splits that reduce training error, we predict a new case by finding its box.
As an intuition, think of a tree as a relative of \(K\)-nearest neighbors with a changing \(k\). The neighborhood is a box rather than a fixed-count window. Its boundaries can adapt to the data. This comparison is useful for understanding the figure, though the two methods choose neighborhoods differently.
For a continuous outcome, the objective is
\[\begin{align}
\min_{R_1, R_2, \dots, R_J} \sum_{j=1}^{J} \sum_{i \in R_j} (y_i - \hat{y}_{R_j})^2
\end{align}\]
Each box \(R_j\) has a mean response. We want to minimize the total squared differences between observations and their box means. Searching all possible partitions is computationally infeasible, so we use recursive partitioning:

Search the features for the split that improves the objective most, and make that split.
Repeat within the new boxes until a stopping rule, such as minimum size or split cost, is reached.

This is a greedy procedure. It chooses the best available split at each step without considering every possible later split. The resulting tree follows locally useful decisions, but is not guaranteed to be the best possible tree.


3.3.4 Two features, and the partition of the space
First, plot the two features together and use color to show the outcome.

ggplot(countries, aes(ppgdp, pctUrban, colour = infantMortality)) +
  geom_point(size = 2)








Each point is a country, located by income and urbanization. Darker points have higher mortality and gather in one corner. The tree will divide this space into rectangles.
With two features, we can still draw the resulting boxes.

t2 <- tree(infantMortality ~ ppgdp + pctUrban, data = countries,
           control = tree.control(nobs = nrow(countries), mindev = 0.002))

partition.tree(t2, main = "The partition of the feature space")








Each rectangle corresponds to a leaf, and its printed number is the prediction for countries in that rectangle. A tree divides the feature space into boxes and assigns one prediction to each.
We use mindev to let the tree grow further than the default. Income already accounts for much of the variation, and tree() otherwise stops splitting quite early.
Again, no rescaling was needed. GDP per capita and percent urban both range to roughly a hundred here, but using income in dollars would only change the axis numbers. The partition would remain identical. This differs from the distance calculation in last week’s model.


3.3.5 A categorical feature, with no dummy coding
The factor group classifies countries as OECD, African, or other. A tree can use it directly.

m_tree3 <- rpart(infantMortality ~ ppgdp + pctUrban + group, data = countries)

rpart.plot(m_tree3, box.palette = "GnBu")








We do not need dummy variables, a reference category, or explicit interaction terms. The tree splits on group membership and prints the category names on the branches.
Check whether group appears in the tree. If it does, compare the income thresholds within the groups. Different thresholds indicate an interaction: the relationship between wealth and mortality varies by group. A linear model would need us to include an interaction term explicitly.
These examples illustrate the first two strengths listed above: handling categories and finding interactions.


3.3.6 Cost complexity, and the parameter that plays the role of k
If allowed to keep splitting, the procedure produces increasingly small, homogeneous leaves and fits the training data closely. Last week showed why we should check whether that improves prediction on new cases.
We can penalize complexity by changing the objective to
\[\begin{align}
C(T, y) = L(T, y) + \alpha |T|
\end{align}\]
Here \(L(T, y)\) is the loss for outcome \(y\) fitted with tree \(T\), and \(|T|\) measures the number of nodes. We want low loss, but also penalize a tree for becoming more complex. The parameter \(\alpha\) sets the strength of that penalty.
A large \(\alpha\) favors a small tree and may leave it too simple to fit the relationship. A small \(\alpha\) allows a larger tree. The role of \(\alpha\) is similar to that of \(k\) in \(K\)-nearest neighbors: like \(k\), it needs to be chosen for the prediction task.
As with last week’s parameter, we use cross-validation to guide the choice.


3.3.7 Pruning
The usual procedure is to grow a large tree, then prune it to a size supported by cross-validation. rpart carries out cross-validation during fitting, so we can inspect its table directly.
To observe the trade-off, we need a tree large enough to overfit. We set cp close to zero and let it grow until leaves contain only a few countries.

set.seed(7)

big_tree <- rpart(infantMortality ~ ppgdp + pctUrban + group,
                  data = countries,
                  control = rpart.control(cp = 0.000001, minsplit = 10,
                                          minbucket = 5, xval = 10))

cpt <- big_tree$cptable

cat("Leaves in the grown tree:", max(cpt[, "nsplit"]) + 1, "\n")

Leaves in the grown tree: 29 


With roughly a hundred and eighty countries and leaves of five, the tree divides the data quite finely. It fits the training observations closely, giving us a useful case for examining overfitting and generalization.
plotcp() displays the cross-validation table, showing error across different tree sizes.

plotcp(big_tree)








There are four things to read in this figure.
The bottom axis shows the complexity parameter on a log scale. Large values are on the left and small ones on the right. A large \(\alpha\) means a stronger penalty and a smaller tree, so complexity increases to the right, as in last week’s \(\log(1/k)\) plot.
The top axis gives the number of leaves. This expresses the same progression in units that are easier to interpret.
The vertical axis shows cross-validated error, scaled relative to a tree with no splits, which has a value of 1. A value of 0.3 means the error is seventy percent lower than predicting the same value for every country.
The vertical bars show one standard error above and below each estimate. The dotted line is one standard error above the minimum error. It supports another selection rule, which we set aside here to use the simpler minimum-error rule.
Read this like last week’s test-error curve. Additional splits initially capture useful structure. Error then levels off and rises as the tree starts fitting individual countries too closely.

3.3.7.1 Choosing where to cut
We choose the tree with the lowest cross-validated error, using the value in the table.

i_min   <- which.min(cpt[, "xerror"])
cp_best <- cpt[i_min, "CP"]

cat("Lowest CV error at", cpt[i_min, "nsplit"] + 1, "leaves, cp =",
    cp_best, "\n")

Lowest CV error at 5 leaves, cp = 0.01229076 


The bottom of this curve is usually fairly flat. Differences between neighboring trees may be smaller than the uncertainty in their error estimates. Treat the minimum as a reasonable choice; nearby trees may perform about as well.

best_tree <- prune(big_tree, cp = cp_best)

rpart.plot(best_tree, box.palette = "GnBu", main = "After pruning")








We have now fitted and pruned a regression tree. Part II changes the outcome to binary, introduces a new dataset, and moves from one row per country to country-year observations.

title: 3  Trees and Random Forests
section: 3.4 Part II. The same idea, on a rare binary outcome
text:
3.4 Part II. The same idea, on a rare binary outcome
The basic procedure carries over to onset. We use majority votes rather than outcome averages within boxes, and a measure of class mixture rather than squared error. Splitting, greediness, complexity penalties, and pruning still apply.
The important changes are the new data, the binary outcome, and especially its rarity. That rarity will shape how we fit and evaluate the model.

url <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/babakrezaee/",
              "AppliedAI-PoliSci/refs/heads/main/data/FearonLaitin2003.csv")

fl <- read.csv(url)

vars <- c("onset", "warl", "gdpenl", "lpopl1", "lmtnest", "ncontig",
          "Oil", "nwstate", "instab", "polity2l", "ethfrac", "relfrac")

cw <- na.omit(fl[, vars])
cw <- cw[cw$onset %in% c(0, 1), ]

nrow(cw)

[1] 6326


In Fearon and Laitin’s data, onset equals 1 when a civil war begins in a country-year.
We use eight covariates from their specification rather than all eleven, to keep the tree legible on a screen. Prior war, non-contiguity, and political instability remain in cw. In the workshop, add them back to the formula and examine how the tree and its readability change.
Watch two details when preparing these data. Oil begins with a capital letter; R distinguishes it from oil. Also, onset occasionally has codes other than 0 and 1 for wars already underway when a country enters the data. We retain only the two values we intend to model.
The country-year structure needs attention. The data cover 1945–1999, so the United States appears fifty-five times. Terrain and colonial history remain the same, and income often changes little between years. Unlike Part I, the observations are repeated within countries. We cannot replace them with country averages because onset occurs in a particular year. We return to the implications at the end of the handout.
First, count how often the outcome occurs.

table(cw$onset)


   0    1 
6221  105 

round(mean(cw$onset), 4)

[1] 0.0166


Civil war begins in roughly two of every hundred country-years. This low base rate is important for interpreting the model’s performance.
Consider a baseline prediction rule that needs no fitting:

Predict that no civil war will begin, anywhere, ever.

This rule is correct about ninety-eight percent of the time. Despite its high accuracy, it misses every war onset. It is therefore unhelpful for identifying the events we want to anticipate.
Keep this baseline for comparison. A more sophisticated model needs to offer something beyond it.

set.seed(7)

n        <- nrow(cw)
train_id <- sample(1:n, floor(0.7 * n))

Train <- cw[train_id, ]
Test  <- cw[-train_id, ]


3.4.1 One tree on onset

m_stump <- rpart(factor(onset) ~ gdpenl + lpopl1 + lmtnest + Oil +
                   nwstate + polity2l + ethfrac + relfrac,
                 data = Train, method = "class",
                 control = rpart.control(cp = 0.004, minbucket = 25))

rpart.plot(m_stump, box.palette = "GnBu")








The tree has not split. It returns one node, predicts no onset for every case, and assigns a probability of 0.02, the base rate we calculated above. Before changing it, consider why this happened.
Under the fitting criterion, a split must improve classification enough to justify its cost. On this rare outcome, the available splits do not improve on predicting no war everywhere. The fitted result is therefore a tree with no splits.
The baseline is not just a difficult comparison: it is what rpart selects with this setup. The software has followed the objective we supplied, but the resulting model does not meet our substantive purpose.

3.4.1.1 Telling the algorithm that the rare class matters
One response is to give the two classes equal importance in fitting, even though they are not equally frequent.

m_class <- rpart(factor(onset) ~ gdpenl + lpopl1 + lmtnest + Oil +
                   nwstate + polity2l + ethfrac + relfrac,
                 data = Train, method = "class",
                 parms   = list(prior = c(0.5, 0.5)),
                 control = rpart.control(cp = 0.002, minbucket = 20))

rpart.plot(m_class, box.palette = "GnBu")








Setting prior this way asks rpart to treat onsets and non-onsets as equally frequent. Each onset then receives roughly fifty times its previous weight, making splits that distinguish wars more useful to the objective. The tree grows. We still use method = "class" and read its branches as before.
There are two points to keep in mind about this change.
First, reweighting is a substantive decision. We chose it because we consider a missed war more costly than a false alarm. The original tree was operating correctly, but our initial objective did not reflect that concern.
Second, we reweight the tree but leave the forest unweighted. This is deliberate, so that we can examine the consequences below.



3.4.2 Why one tree is not enough
A single tree can be unstable: small changes in the training data may lead to a substantially different tree.

par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

set.seed(7)

for (i in 1:3) {
  draw <- Train[sample(1:nrow(Train), nrow(Train), replace = TRUE), ]

  t_i <- rpart(factor(onset) ~ gdpenl + lpopl1 + lmtnest + Oil +
                 nwstate + polity2l + ethfrac + relfrac,
               data = draw, method = "class",
               parms   = list(prior = c(0.5, 0.5)),
               control = rpart.control(cp = 0.004, minbucket = 20))

  rpart.plot(t_i, box.palette = "GnBu", main = paste("Sample", i))
}








Compare the first splits in these three trees, each fitted to a sample from the same data. A different first split changes the cases reaching each branch, and therefore changes the later splits too.
This is variance, the term we introduced last week. A deep tree can represent many shapes and thus have low bias, but the shape it selects may depend heavily on the sample. Greedy splitting adds to this instability because an early decision affects all the branches below it.
Although a single tree is easy to read, its instability motivates combining several trees.


3.4.3 From bagging to random forests
Bagging, short for bootstrap aggregating, fits trees to repeated samples drawn with replacement and combines their predictions. This takes more computation than fitting one tree. Averaging reduces variation when the trees’ errors are not all the same.
Random forests add another source of randomization. At each split, a tree considers a sampled subset of \(m\) variables rather than all the features.
Suppose income is the strongest predictor. Bagged trees may repeatedly split on it, producing similar trees with correlated errors. Restricting the available features at each split makes the trees less alike. Individual trees may become worse, while their combined prediction improves because their errors are less correlated.
The aim is to combine many imperfect trees whose errors differ, rather than to find one exceptionally good tree.
Two parameters matter: \(B\), the number of bootstrapped trees, and \(m\), the number of features available at each split. A common choice is \(m = \sqrt{p}\), with \(p\) the total feature count. When \(m = p\), the procedure reduces to bagging.


3.4.4 Fitting the forest
We now change the method argument in last week’s caret setup.

Train$onset_f <- factor(ifelse(Train$onset == 1, "war", "no_war"),
                        levels = c("no_war", "war"))
Test$onset_f  <- factor(ifelse(Test$onset == 1, "war", "no_war"),
                        levels = c("no_war", "war"))

set.seed(7)

rf <- train(onset_f ~ gdpenl + lpopl1 + lmtnest + Oil +
              nwstate + polity2l + ethfrac + relfrac,
            data      = Train,
            method    = "rf",
            ntree     = 300,
            trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5),
            tuneGrid  = data.frame(mtry = c(2, 3, 5)))

rf

  mtry  Accuracy   Kappa       
  2     0.9805785  -0.003979084
  3     0.9794498  -0.005356815
  5     0.9789981  -0.005866209

Accuracy was used to select the optimal model using the largest value.
The final value used for the model was mtry = 2.


The structure is familiar: a formula, training data, cross-validation, and a tuning grid. The new arguments are method = "rf" and the grid for mtry. We convert the outcome to a factor to request classification. Feature rescaling is unnecessary here.
We have not included class weighting or a prior argument in this call. Unlike the single tree, the forest receives no instruction to give onset extra weight. We will examine the effect of leaving it that way.
Allow a minute or two for this chunk to run.

3.4.4.1 Predicting for cases the model has never seen
After tuning, train() refits the selected model on the full training set. We can predict directly from the resulting object.

pred <- predict(rf, newdata = Test)

head(pred)

[1] no_war no_war no_war no_war no_war no_war
Levels: no_war war


Use rf for prediction rather than rf$finalModel. The caret object retains information about preprocessing that the underlying fitted model does not. Calling the underlying model directly can therefore bypass transformations needed for new data.



3.4.5 The accuracy trap

cm <- table(Predicted = pred, Actual = Test$onset_f)
cm

         Actual
Predicted no_war  war
   no_war   1865   30
   war         3    0

accuracy <- sum(diag(cm)) / sum(cm)
round(accuracy, 4)

[1] 0.9826


The accuracy is high. Taken on its own, it could make this model look successful.
Compare it with the baseline that always predicts no onset.

baseline <- mean(Test$onset_f == "no_war")
round(baseline, 4)

[1] 0.9842


The improvement over that baseline is small or absent, despite growing nine hundred trees and tuning mtry by cross-validation.
Now inspect the confusion matrix. Among the actual wars, how many did the forest predict? It identifies close to none.
The forest is operating as specified. We selected on accuracy, which gives little incentive to identify an outcome occurring in only two percent of cases.
The result resembles the initial tree with no splits. We reweighted that tree to make onset matter more, but left the forest unchanged. Read the two results together: the objective matters as well as the algorithm. caret selected mtry to maximize accuracy, even though accuracy did not adequately reflect our interest in war onset.
The output gave no warning about this mismatch. Cross-validation ran correctly and the test set was held out, yet the resulting model failed to identify the outcome we wanted to predict. Following those procedures was not enough to make the model useful.
This is the problem addressed by the second reading (Muchlinski et al. 2016). Week 6 covers precision, recall, F1, thresholds, and class weighting in more detail, including how unequal error costs affect evaluation. For now, focus on recognizing the problem.

3.4.5.1 The four cells
The table is a confusion matrix. To name its cells, we first choose the positive class. Here it is war onset; this is an analyst’s choice rather than a property of the data.




Actually war
Actually no war




Predicted war
True positive
False positive


Predicted no war
False negative
True negative



A false positive flags onset in a country-year where none occurs. A false negative misses an onset that does occur. Their consequences differ, so deciding which matters more requires a political and ethical judgment. Accuracy combines them without expressing that judgment explicitly.



3.4.6 Variable importance, and what it does not mean
We cannot read a forest like an individual tree, but we can examine variable importance.

varImpPlot(rf$finalModel, main = "Variable importance")








Importance measures how much the model relies on a feature. One approach totals improvements from splits using that feature; another permutes its values and measures the loss in predictive performance. A feature whose values can be shuffled without affecting performance contributes little under that measure.
Across the bootstrapped trees, useful features tend to be selected and used more often. The ranking summarizes their contribution to the fitted forest.
Interpret this plot with several limitations in mind.
Importance is not effect size. Its units do not have a direct substantive interpretation. Twice the importance does not mean twice the influence, and the values are not directly comparable across models or datasets.
Importance has no sign. A high ranking does not tell us whether income raises or lowers predicted onset risk. It also cannot distinguish a positive relationship from a negative or U-shaped one.
Correlated features can share importance. If features provide similar information, the forest may use them interchangeably, reducing the importance assigned to each. A low ranking may therefore reflect overlap rather than irrelevance. Income, population, and regime measures in these data are related, so consider that possibility here.
Impurity-based importance favors features with many distinct values. Continuous variables may rank above binary ones partly for this reason. Compare the binary features Oil and nwstate with gdpenl.
Importance does not establish causation. It describes the predictors the forest used, without estimating what would happen if we changed them.
Policy briefs and press coverage sometimes present importance rankings as the drivers of a problem. We can make a narrower claim: these features were useful for prediction in this fitted model on this dataset. Explaining causes requires additional evidence.

title: 3  Trees and Random Forests
text:
3.5 Prediction, forecasting, and early warning
Week 1 distinguished prediction from forecasting. So far we have predicted country-years randomly held out from the same historical period as the training data. We have not forecast future events.
The third reading describes ViEWS (Hegre et al. 2019), which issues monthly forecasts of political violence before the target months occur. This requires a different evaluation setup.
For forecasting, we need to split by time. Training on 1995 and 1999 to predict 1997 gives the model information from after the target year. Training up to a date and testing beyond it better reflects the information available when forecasting. Looking ahead can make a model appear more successful than it would be in practice.
The country-year structure introduces another issue. Sudan in 1996 is related to Sudan in 1995, so putting one in a test fold and the other in training can let closely related information cross the split. Standard cross-validation treats observations as interchangeable, which does not fit this structure. We return to the problem and possible responses in Week 6.

title: 3  Trees and Random Forests
text:
3.6 The politics of early warning
Forecasts are often produced to guide action. Their intended use therefore matters when assessing errors.
Flagging a country as high risk may influence investment, aid, insurance, travel advice, diplomacy, or arguments for intervention. A forecast can become part of the political situation it describes.
With an outcome occurring in two percent of cases, even good discrimination can produce many false alarms because non-events are so numerous. A country may bear the costs of being flagged even when no onset follows. We can assess that outcome only after the forecast period has passed.
Forecasts may also affect the outcome. For example, a warning might cause investment to fall, which could increase instability. The forecast could then appear more accurate partly because people acted on it. This possibility needs attention when evaluating predictions used in political decisions.
Last week we asked who defines similarity. Here we should ask who chooses the threshold for a warning. Turning forest votes into a flag on a map requires a cut point that affects false alarms and missed wars. Who selects it, how is it justified, and do those bearing the consequences have a say?

title: 3  Trees and Random Forests
text:
3.7 Reading
Fearon, J. D., and Laitin, D. D. 2003. “Ethnicity, Insurgency, and Civil War.” American Political Science Review 97(1): 75–90. (Fearon and Laitin 2003)
Read this article for its explanation of civil war and the specification behind our data. Its authors seek to explain onset, whereas we use the data for prediction. Keep that difference in mind as you compare their analysis with ours.
Muchlinski, D., Siroky, D., He, J., and Kocher, M. 2016. “Comparing Random Forest with Logistic Regression for Predicting Class-Imbalanced Civil War Onset Data.” Political Analysis 24(1): 87–103. (Muchlinski et al. 2016)
Focus on the treatment of rare outcomes rather than the implementation. If time permits, read the critical exchange it prompted as well. It raises useful questions about what model-performance comparisons can establish.
Hegre, H., et al. 2019. “ViEWS: A Political Violence Early-Warning System.” Journal of Peace Research 56(2): 155–174. (Hegre et al. 2019)
Read this as an account of an early-warning system in use. Pay particular attention to how the forecasts should be interpreted and who is expected to use them.
Recommended, not required.
Pinckney, J., and RezaeeDaryakenari, B. 2022. “When the Levee Breaks: A Forecasting Model of Violent and Nonviolent Dissent.” International Interactions 48(5): 997–1026. (Pinckney and RezaeeDaryakenari 2022)
This article forecasts armed and unarmed conflict at the country-year level using eight algorithms and five forecasting ensembles. Compare its ensembles with our forest: both combine predictions from models whose errors may differ. Also consider how including nonviolent mobilization changes the task, since unarmed uprisings are less rare than civil war and their measurement presents different difficulties.

text:
3.9 Questions for the session
Prepare an answer to at least two questions.

Fearon and Laitin set out to explain civil war, whereas we used their variables to predict it. What did we learn that they did not, and what did they establish that our model cannot?
A single tree is easy to read but can be unstable; a forest can improve prediction while being harder to interpret. Which concern matters more for political science? Does your answer depend on the model’s purpose?
The forest deliberately makes each tree worse, by withholding features from it, in order that the ensemble should be better. Is there anything analogous in the way political institutions aggregate judgments? Committees, juries, federal structures, and multiple veto players are all admissible.
Our model achieved very high accuracy and predicted almost no wars, and every technical step was performed correctly. What does this suggest about the relationship between methodological correctness and usefulness?
Variable importance is regularly reported in policy documents as identifying the drivers of a problem. Write the one sentence you would add to such a document in order to make it honest, and state what would be lost in the process.
Who should select the threshold at which a forecast becomes a warning, and to whom should that selection be explained? Note that those bearing the cost of a false alarm and those bearing the cost of a missed war are generally not the same people.

title: 4  Text as Data: Naive Bayes
text:
4.1 What Naive Bayes is good at, and what it is not
Week 4, 23 September
Until now, our datasets came with features already prepared. The UN data included income and urbanization, and Fearon and Laitin supplied measured and coded covariates. We began modeling after those measurement decisions had been made.
This week we start with 905 tweets. Before fitting a model, we need to turn their text into features. The choices involved are part of the analysis: they determine which information the classifier can use and can account for many of its errors.
We will use Naive Bayes. It assumes something about language that is clearly false, yet can still classify text effectively. In the second half of the session, we will examine how that is possible.
Benefits.
There are two important limitations.
First, the method assumes conditional independence between words. We will discuss why that assumption does not describe language well.
Second, the labels come from human coding decisions. Our classifier learns to reproduce one person’s application of a scheme for identifying immigration tweets. It does not independently define immigration, and any arbitrary parts of the coding scheme also shape its training.

It fits by counting rather than optimization, so it is fast and can handle vocabularies of tens of thousands of words.
It can perform well with small training sets, useful when people must read and label every training document.

It returns probabilities that can be turned into classifications using a threshold suited to the task.
