section: 4.3 Part I. From tweets to a matrix
text:
4.3 Part I. From tweets to a matrix

4.3.1 Reading the text before modeling it
Before building a text model, read some of the documents.

for (i in 1:4) {
  cat(as.character(tweets$label[i]), "|", tweets$text[i], "\n\n")
}

other | ....the FBI was in complete turmoil (see N.Y. Post) because of Comey’s poor leadership and the way he handled the Clinton mess (not to mention his usurpation of powers from the Justice Department). My firing of James Comey was a great day for America. He was a Crooked Cop...... 

other | Do you remember two years ago when Iraq was going to fight the Kurds in a different part of Syria. Many people wanted us to fight with the Kurds against Iraq, who we just fought for. I said no, and the Kurds left the fight, twice. Now the same thing is happening with Turkey...... 

immigration | The failed Fast Train project in California, where the cost overruns are becoming world record setting, is hundreds of times more expensive than the desperately needed Wall! 

immigration | Democrats had to quickly take down a tweet called “Kids In Cages, Inhumane Treatment at the Border,” because the horrible picture used was from the Obama years. Very embarrassing! @foxandfriends 


These four tweets show several things we will need to address: URLs, handles beginning with @, capitals used for emphasis, and curly quotation marks that R treats differently from straight ones. At least one label is also open to reasonable disagreement.


4.3.2 The bag of words
We will use a simple representation. First, consider what it leaves out.
We represent each document by the words it contains, discarding order, grammar, and the relationships between words. “The wall stopped the caravan” and “the caravan stopped the wall” therefore have the same representation.
This is the bag of words approach: we retain the words and their counts, as though they had been mixed together in a bag.
Whether this is adequate depends on the research question. For detecting immigration content, words such as border, caravan, and asylum are often useful regardless of order. A question about who did what to whom would require a representation that preserves more of the relationships between words.


4.3.3 Cleaning, one decision at a time
The tm package stores documents in a corpus.

corpus <- VCorpus(VectorSource(tweets$text))

corpus[[1]]$content

[1] "....the FBI was in complete turmoil (see N.Y. Post) because of Comey’s poor leadership and the way he handled the Clinton mess (not to mention his usurpation of powers from the Justice Department). My firing of James Comey was a great day for America. He was a Crooked Cop......"


tm_map() applies a transformation to the corpus and returns the transformed corpus. We need to build one transformation ourselves to remove a pattern from the text.

replace_with_space <- content_transformer(function(x, pattern) {
  gsub(pattern, " ", x)
})

content_transformer() wraps our character-string function so that tm_map() can apply it to individual documents. Use this wrapper when creating your own cleaning function.

clean <- tm_map(corpus, content_transformer(tolower))
clean <- tm_map(clean, replace_with_space, "http[s]?://\\S*")
clean <- tm_map(clean, replace_with_space, "@\\S+")
clean <- tm_map(clean, replace_with_space, "[^a-z ]")
clean <- tm_map(clean, removeWords, stopwords("english"))
clean <- tm_map(clean, stemDocument)
clean <- tm_map(clean, stripWhitespace)

clean[[1]]$content

[1] "fbi complet turmoil see n y post comey s poor leadership way handl clinton mess mention usurp power justic depart fire jame comey great day america crook cop"


Here are the seven cleaning steps and the choices they involve.
Lowercasing combines Wall and wall, which we want, but also US and us, which we might want to keep separate. A general lowercasing rule cannot distinguish them.
Removing URLs and handles simplifies the text but can remove useful information. For example, @ThomasHomanICE, the acting director of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, is highly informative about a tweet’s subject. We omit it for a simple pipeline. In the workshop, you could test whether retaining handles improves classification.
[^a-z ] removes everything except lowercase letters and spaces: punctuation, digits, emoji, and the curly quotation marks and en dashes left behind by removePunctuation(). Without this step, some features appear in the output as codes such as <U+2019>, which can be confusing to interpret.
Stopwords are words such as the, and, of, and is, which usually carry little topical information. Inspect the supplied list with head(stopwords("english"), 50). It includes not and against, both of which can be important in political text.
Stemming combines inflected forms: immigration, immigrants, and immigrate become immigr. This pools sparse features, but the resulting stems are not ordinary words and some combinations may be unsuitable.
Whitespace cleanup is cosmetic. Unlike the other steps, it does not make a substantive choice about which information to retain.
The order of cleaning steps also matters. Removing punctuation first changes don't to dont, so it no longer matches the stopword don't. Reversing the steps changes the vocabulary. Denny and Spirling (Denny and Spirling 2018) show why preprocessing deserves more attention than a brief sentence in an appendix: these decisions can change substantive results.


4.3.4 The document-term matrix

dtm <- DocumentTermMatrix(clean)

dtm

<<DocumentTermMatrix (documents: 905, terms: 2735)>>
Non-/sparse entries: 16606/2458569
Sparsity           : 99%
Maximal term length: 16
Weighting          : term frequency (tf)


The document-term matrix has one row per document and one column per term. Entry \(i\), \(j\) counts how often term \(j\) occurs in document \(i\).
There are close to three thousand terms across 905 tweets, so we have more columns than rows. The matrix is also 99 percent sparse: most cells are zero, since a tweet uses only around fifteen of the available words.
These properties are common in text data. They create difficulties for a conventional regression with three thousand predictors and nine hundred observations. Naive Bayes handles them through the assumption introduced below.


4.3.5 What is in the corpus
Compare the vocabulary in the two classes before fitting the model.

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0))

set.seed(7)

wordcloud(clean[tweets$label == "immigration"], min.freq = 12,
          random.order = FALSE, colors = brewer.pal(7, "Blues")[3:7])
title("immigration")

wordcloud(clean[tweets$label == "other"], min.freq = 12,
          random.order = FALSE, colors = brewer.pal(7, "Oranges")[3:7])
title("other")








Word clouds are useful for an initial look, though poor for inference: areas are hard to compare accurately, and the layout is random.
As expected, border and wall dominate the immigration cloud. But illeg appears in both classes because the negative class includes tweets about illegal wiretaps and impeachments. democrat is common in both because Trump attacks Democrats on many subjects. These near misses were included deliberately, so a single keyword is not enough to classify the corpus.


4.3.6 Splitting before anything else
The rows were shuffled before the file was distributed. Splitting by row number therefore gives an approximately random division.

n <- nrow(tweets)

train_id <- 1:floor(0.8 * n)

dtm_train <- dtm[train_id, ]
dtm_test  <- dtm[-train_id, ]

y_train <- tweets$label[train_id]
y_test  <- tweets$label[-train_id]

c(train = length(y_train), test = length(y_test))

train  test 
  724   181 

round(prop.table(table(y_train)), 3)

y_train
      other immigration 
      0.613       0.387 

round(prop.table(table(y_test)), 3)

y_test
      other immigration 
      0.519       0.481 


The class proportions differ somewhat between the two sets. Use the test-set majority proportion as the baseline for test-set accuracy.
Split before selecting the vocabulary. We choose which words to retain using training data only. Selecting them from all 905 tweets would use information from the test set before evaluation, potentially making the score optimistic without an obvious warning in the output.


4.3.7 Trimming the vocabulary
Most terms appear only once or twice. They add many features while providing little evidence for generalization.

freq_words <- findFreqTerms(dtm_train, 5)

length(freq_words)

[1] 651

head(freq_words, 24)

 [1] "abl"       "absolut"   "abus"      "act"       "action"    "actual"   
 [7] "adam"      "administr" "african"   "agenda"    "agent"     "ago"      
[13] "agre"      "agreement" "aid"       "alien"     "allow"     "almost"   
[19] "along"     "alreadi"   "also"      "alway"     "amend"     "america"  


Requiring at least five occurrences in the training documents removes roughly three quarters of the vocabulary. Five is a conventional choice, not a uniquely correct threshold. Like \(k\) in Week 2 and the complexity parameter in Week 3, this choice could be guided by cross-validation. Try changing it in the workshop.

dtm_train <- dtm_train[, freq_words]
dtm_test  <- dtm_test[, freq_words]

Use the training vocabulary for the test matrix too. Words seen only in the test set are excluded because the fitted model has no training information about them.


4.3.8 The counts stay as counts
We keep the entries as counts: each cell records how many times a word occurs in a tweet.

counts_train <- as.matrix(dtm_train)
counts_test  <- as.matrix(dtm_test)

dim(counts_train)

[1] 724 651

counts_train[1:3, 1:6]

    Terms
Docs abl absolut abus act action actual
   1   0       0    0   0      0      0
   2   0       0    0   0      0      0
   3   0       0    0   0      0      0


as.matrix() turns tm’s compressed representation into an ordinary R matrix, which is convenient at this size. For a corpus of a hundred thousand documents, memory requirements could make it necessary to retain the compressed form.


4.3.9 Two rates per word
We can now compare how often each word appears in the two classes. This calculation provides most of the quantities the classifier will need.

total_immigration <- colSums(counts_train[y_train == "immigration", ])
total_other       <- colSums(counts_train[y_train == "other", ])

totals <- data.frame(word        = freq_words,
                     immigration = total_immigration,
                     other       = total_other)

head(totals[order(-totals$immigration), 2:3], 12)

         immigration other
border           237    49
wall             131    12
will             111   140
democrat          90    51
immigr            67     5
mexico            66    34
southern          63     1
countri           62    38
secur             62    13
illeg             54    51
great             52   124
want              46    22


In the training data, border appears 237 times in immigration tweets and 49 times in other tweets.
To compare these counts, we need to account for differences in the groups’ size and total quantity of text.

sum(total_immigration)

[1] 4786

sum(total_other)

[1] 6395


The immigration class contains fewer words overall. Divide each count by its class total to obtain a rate: how many occurrences of this word are there per thousand words in that class?

rate_immigration <- 1000 * total_immigration / sum(total_immigration)
rate_other       <- 1000 * total_other       / sum(total_other)

rates <- data.frame(word        = freq_words,
                    immigration = rate_immigration,
                    other       = rate_other)

round(head(rates[order(-rates$immigration), 2:3], 12), 2)

         immigration other
border         49.52  7.66
wall           27.37  1.88
will           23.19 21.89
democrat       18.80  7.97
immigr         14.00  0.78
mexico         13.79  5.32
southern       13.16  0.16
countri        12.95  5.94
secur          12.95  2.03
illeg          11.28  7.97
great          10.87 19.39
want            9.61  3.44


Read the first row conditionally. Within immigration tweets, about 50 words per thousand are border. Within the other tweets, about 8 are.
This is a conditional probability: a rate within a subgroup. We are asking how common border is within each class, rather than across the corpus as a whole. Naive Bayes uses these class-specific proportions, which we can calculate from colSums().

ggplot(rates, aes(other, immigration)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "gray60", linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(data = subset(rates, immigration > 6 | other > 6),
            aes(label = word), size = 3, vjust = -0.6) +
  labs(x = "Uses per 1,000 words in *other* tweets",
       y = "Uses per 1,000 words in *immigration* tweets")








The dashed line marks equal rates. A word on that line does not help distinguish the classes. Words farther from it provide more information, and the side of the line indicates which label they favor.
Most words are rare in both classes and cluster near the origin. Above the line are border, wall, southern, secur, and immigr, which favor immigration. Below it are words such as great, presid, and thank, which favor the other class. will is common in both and contributes little to distinguishing them.
We have not fitted the classifier yet, but this plot shows the rate comparison it will use.

title: 4  Text as Data: Naive Bayes
text:
4.4 Part II. Naive Bayes

4.4.1 The question the model asks
Given a tweet’s words, how likely is it to be about immigration? That is the question we want to answer.
Estimating every possible combination of words directly would require much more than our 724 training tweets. Most combinations have never appeared in those data.
Instead, we calculate how likely the words are under each label. The rates above provide those quantities, which we can compare to work back toward the label.
For a tweet containing border and wall:

Under the immigration label, these words are relatively common: about 50 and 27 occurrences per thousand words, respectively.
Under the other label, their rates are much lower: about 8 and 2 per thousand.

These words favor immigration. Bayes’ rule lets us use word probabilities conditional on a label to infer label probabilities conditional on the words. It also accounts for the relative frequency of the labels, so a rare label needs stronger evidence. We will use this intuition here; the further reading provides the algebra.


4.4.2 The naive assumption, which is false
We still need a way to calculate the probability of a whole combination of words. Naive Bayes simplifies this by assuming:

Assume that, within a class, each word appears independently of every other.

Under this assumption, knowing that an immigration tweet contains southern would tell us nothing further about whether it contains border.
That does not fit the language in this corpus. Southern and border often appear together, as do illegal and immigration, and caravan and migrant. Words are related to one another.
The assumption is useful computationally because it lets us multiply separate word rates instead of estimating the probability of every word combination. We can estimate those rates from a few hundred documents.
One consequence is overconfidence. A tweet with border, southern, wall, and patrol supplies correlated evidence, but the model treats the words as four independent signals. Its probabilities can therefore cluster near 0 and 1. Useful rankings do not imply calibrated probabilities. We may use these scores to order documents while being cautious about interpreting their confidence literally.


4.4.3 Words that never occurred
Before fitting, consider words that occur in one training class but never in the other.

never_in_other <- names(which(total_other == 0))

length(never_in_other)

[1] 21

never_in_other

 [1] "aid"          "alien"        "apprehend"    "build"        "caravan"     
 [6] "census"       "citizenship"  "cross"        "daca"         "deport"      
[11] "emerg"        "expens"       "humanitarian" "migrant"      "progress"    
[16] "reduc"        "renov"        "schumer"      "section"      "solv"        
[21] "stay"        


Twenty-one words occur in immigration tweets but never in other tweets. Some are unsurprising, such as caravan, deport, daca, and migrant. Others, including stay and progress, may be absent from the other class simply by chance.
Their estimated rate in other would be zero. Since the model multiplies rates, one zero would make the whole product zero: caravan alone would rule out other, regardless of the remaining thirty words. Six thousand words of training text do not justify that certainty. Laplace smoothing adds one occurrence of every word to each class before calculating rates, preventing a single unobserved word from ruling a class out.


4.4.4 Fitting
Fitting takes two lines using the counts we have already calculated.

p_immigration <- (total_immigration + 1) / sum(total_immigration + 1)
p_other       <- (total_other + 1) / sum(total_other + 1)

Each vector gives the vocabulary’s word proportions within one class. The + 1 applies smoothing. Including it in the denominator keeps each vector’s entries summing to one.
We also need the prior probabilities: how common each label is. Without informative words, the model should favor the more common label.

prior_immigration <- mean(y_train == "immigration")
prior_other       <- mean(y_train == "other")

round(c(other = prior_other, immigration = prior_immigration), 3)

      other immigration 
      0.613       0.387 


The model consists of two word-rate tables and two prior probabilities. There is no iterative optimization or convergence step, and no random seed needed for the fit. Unlike last week’s forest, we can inspect these fitted quantities directly.

round(1000 * c(immigration = p_immigration[["border"]],
               other       = p_other[["border"]]), 2)

immigration       other 
      43.77        7.10 

round(1000 * c(immigration = p_immigration[["great"]],
               other       = p_other[["great"]]), 2)

immigration       other 
       9.75       17.74 

round(1000 * c(immigration = p_immigration[["caravan"]],
               other       = p_other[["caravan"]]), 2)

immigration       other 
       2.02        0.14 


border favors immigration, while great favors other. Smoothing gives caravan a small nonzero rate in other, so a tweet mentioning caravans can still receive that label if its remaining words support it strongly enough.






Note



The e1071 package provides naiveBayes(), but numeric matrix inputs are treated as normally distributed within each class. That is unsuitable for these word counts, most of which are zero; on this matrix it classifies almost every tweet as immigration. The calculations above implement the text-count version of Naive Bayes explicitly.




4.4.5 Predicting
For a new tweet, compare how well the two rate tables account for its words and assign the label with the higher score.

score_immigration <- as.vector(counts_test %*% log(p_immigration)) +
  log(prior_immigration)

score_other <- as.vector(counts_test %*% log(p_other)) +
  log(prior_other)

pred <- factor(ifelse(score_immigration > score_other, "immigration", "other"),
               levels = c("other", "immigration"))

head(pred)

[1] other       other       immigration other       immigration other      
Levels: other immigration


For each tweet, the matrix multiplication adds a word’s log rate under a label once per occurrence. Using border four times therefore contributes four times as much evidence as using it once. This is why we retained counts rather than just presence or absence.
Multiplying hundreds of small probabilities risks numerical underflow. Adding their logarithms avoids that problem while preserving the ordering of the scores, which is what we use for classification.


4.4.6 The confusion matrix

cm <- table(Predicted = pred, Actual = y_test)

cm

             Actual
Predicted     other immigration
  other          82           5
  immigration    12          82

accuracy <- sum(diag(cm)) / sum(cm)
round(accuracy, 4)

[1] 0.9061

baseline <- mean(y_test == "other")
round(baseline, 4)

[1] 0.5193


The model gets roughly 90 percent correct, compared with a baseline of roughly 52 percent. That is a much larger improvement than we saw last week.
Remember which data this score describes. The corpus was assembled to make the classes comparable in size. Immigration tweets are a minority of Trump’s full 2019 output, and the remaining tweets cover more varied subjects than our negative class. Applying the classifier to that stream would create more opportunities for false alarms and reduce performance.
Inspect the confusion matrix as well as the overall score.

confusionMatrix(pred, y_test, positive = "immigration")

Confusion Matrix and Statistics

             Reference
Prediction    other immigration
  other          82           5
  immigration    12          82
                                             
               Accuracy : 0.9061             
                 95% CI : (0.8539, 0.9443)   
    No Information Rate : 0.5193             
    P-Value [Acc > NIR] : <0.0000000000000002
                                             
                  Kappa : 0.8124             
                                             
 Mcnemar's Test P-Value : 0.1456             
                                             
            Sensitivity : 0.9425             
            Specificity : 0.8723             
         Pos Pred Value : 0.8723             
         Neg Pred Value : 0.9425             
             Prevalence : 0.4807             
         Detection Rate : 0.4530             
   Detection Prevalence : 0.5193             
      Balanced Accuracy : 0.9074             
                                             
       'Positive' Class : immigration        
                                             


caret reports several useful quantities. We introduce three here and return to them in Week 6.
No Information Rate is the majority-class baseline, accompanied by a test of whether the model beats it.
Sensitivity, or recall, is the proportion of immigration tweets the model identifies. Here it catches almost all of them.
Positive predictive value, or precision, is the proportion of flagged tweets that are genuinely about immigration. It is lower here: the model tends to over-flag rather than miss borderline cases.
Their relative importance depends on the task. If we want to estimate the immigration share of Trump’s output, false positives inflate it, making precision important. If we want to retrieve tweets for someone to read, recall may matter more, because false positives mainly add reading time.


4.4.7 The most informative words
For each word, compare its rates across the two classes. Using a log ratio puts evidence in both directions on a symmetric scale.

log_ratio <- sort(log(p_immigration / p_other))

top <- c(head(log_ratio, 12), tail(log_ratio, 12))

par(mar = c(4, 7, 3, 2))

barplot(top, horiz = TRUE, las = 1, cex.names = 0.8,
        col = ifelse(top > 0, "steelblue", "darkorange"),
        xlab = "log ratio, immigration versus other",
        main = "The words that move the classifier")








Unlike the forest’s importance ranking, this plot shows direction as well as strength. southern, apprehend, caravan, alien, humanitarian, and loophol favor immigration. impeach, witch, hunt, collus, and mueller favor the other class.
The orange words show a limitation. Impeachment and the Mueller investigation are not conceptually the opposite of immigration; they were other subjects Trump discussed in 2019. The classifier learns that distinction from this corpus. We should not assume it will transfer to another year or author.


4.4.8 Reading the errors
Fewer than twenty test tweets were misclassified. Read them to understand the errors behind the score.

test_text <- tweets$text[-train_id]

wrong <- which(pred != y_test)

length(wrong)

[1] 17

for (i in head(wrong, 6)) {
  cat("actual:", as.character(y_test[i]),
      "| predicted:", as.character(pred[i]), "\n",
      substr(test_text[i], 1, 180), "\n\n")
}

actual: other | predicted: immigration 
 Everyone very excited about the new deal with Mexico! 

actual: immigration | predicted: other 
 While the reviews and reporting on our Border Immigration Agreement with Mexico have been very good, there has nevertheless been much false reporting (surprise!) by the Fake and Co 

actual: other | predicted: immigration 
 “This is not Congressional Oversight, this is bullying.” Jason Riley, The Wall Street Journal 

actual: other | predicted: immigration 
 Kevin Corke, @FoxNews “Don’t forget, Michael Cohen has already been convicted of perjury and fraud, and as recently as this week, the Wall Street Journal has suggested that he may  

actual: immigration | predicted: other 
 Our Border Control Agents have done an incredible job under very adverse conditions. I am very proud to have increased their salaries because of the great job they do. Nobody deser 

actual: other | predicted: immigration 
 As Corey Lewandowski stated very clearly yesterday in front of the House Judiciary Committee, President Trump didn’t do anything wrong or illegal. But they all know that. The Democ 


Several patterns appear in these errors.
Two of the six tweets concern the Wall Street Journal, which triggers wall. Another uses illegal in a different context, triggering illeg. A bag of individual words cannot distinguish the phrase Wall Street from the border-wall vocabulary.
Two errors go the other way. A tweet about reporting on the Border Immigration Agreement with Mexico uses the language of media attacks. Another praises Border Control agents for a great job, using a strong other word. Both concern immigration, but their vocabulary favors the other label.
Remove head() to inspect the remaining eleven errors. One endorsement describes Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith as strong on the border and illegal immigration. The codebook labels endorsement boilerplate other, treating the border as one item in a formula. The model disagrees with that contestable rule. Another tweet thanks @DHSgov, @CBP, and @ICEgov. After removing the handles, little remains beyond thank you, and the model predicts other despite the immigration label.
These patterns suggest different responses: include word pairs to distinguish Wall Street, retain informative handles, and reconsider how to represent endorsement boilerplate. A bag of words alone cannot resolve that coding distinction.


4.4.9 The same model in caret
We wrote the calculations ourselves so you could see how the classifier works. For your own projects, a package is more convenient. We will use caret, as we did for the forest.
method = "naive_bayes" calls the naivebayes package, which needs to be installed.

install.packages("naivebayes")

We first change the features to two-level factors recording whether each word is present. As noted above, these functions otherwise treat numeric columns as normally distributed within classes, which poorly describes our mostly zero word counts.

as_yes_no <- function(counts) {
  out <- as.data.frame(counts > 0)
  out[] <- lapply(out, function(x) {
    factor(x, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE), labels = c("No", "Yes"))
  })
  out
}

X_train <- as_yes_no(counts_train)
X_test  <- as_yes_no(counts_test)

X_train[1:3, 1:5]

  abl absolut abus act action
1  No      No   No  No     No
2  No      No   No  No     No
3  No      No   No  No     No


We set the two factor levels explicitly. Otherwise, a word absent from every test tweet would have only one level in the test data, and predict() would reject the mismatch.

set.seed(7)

nb_caret <- train(x = X_train, y = y_train,
                  method    = "naive_bayes",
                  trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5),
                  tuneGrid  = expand.grid(laplace   = c(0, 1),
                                          usekernel = FALSE,
                                          adjust    = 1))

nb_caret

The call follows the same structure as Week 3: inputs, a resampling scheme, and a tuning grid. Smoothing is now a parameter selected by cross-validation between laplace = 0 and laplace = 1, using training data only.

pred_caret <- predict(nb_caret, X_test)

confusionMatrix(pred_caret, y_test, positive = "immigration")

Confusion Matrix and Statistics

Accuracy is slightly below our count-based model. This version records whether border occurs, whereas our earlier model also uses how often it occurs. Repetition carries extra evidence in the count model. That difference is small for short tweets but can matter more in longer documents.
Using caret gives us cross-validation, a tuning grid, and a familiar interface. The underlying calculations are now inside an object rather than displayed as word-rate tables, so we need to make a more deliberate effort to inspect them.

title: 4  Text as Data: Naive Bayes
text:
4.5 The politics of classification
The classification tasks in this course sort cases into categories. For political text, those categories concern speech.
Our classifier reads political speech and assigns a topic. Similar classification tasks appear in content moderation, media monitoring, and state surveillance. Thinking about those uses helps us see why even this small teaching example raises political questions.
Consider two aspects of the model we built.
First, someone chose immigration and other as the categories. The model cannot determine whether that was the right distinction for the research question. High accuracy does not justify the choice of categories.
Second, the errors have a pattern. False positives include tweets using immigration vocabulary for another purpose. In deployed systems, such patterns affect particular forms of speech and the people who use them. The consequences differ greatly between a measurement error in a paper and a classification that triggers a takedown, investigation, or visit.
We have asked who defines similarity and who selects the warning threshold. Here, ask who writes the codebook. Those decisions shape the model before fitting and may be difficult to see in its output.

title: 4  Text as Data: Naive Bayes
text:
4.6 Reading
Grimmer, J., and Stewart, B. M. 2013. “Text as Data: The Promise and Pitfalls of Automatic Content Analysis Methods for Political Texts.” Political Analysis 21(3): 267–297. (Grimmer and Stewart 2013)
This article introduces the field and several principles we have used: language models simplify language, no method is best for every task, and validation is essential. Read its discussion of supervised methods alongside Part II, paying attention to the problems it asks researchers to check.
Denny, M. J., and Spirling, A. 2018. “Text Preprocessing For Unsupervised Learning: Why It Matters, When It Misleads, and What To Do About It.” Political Analysis 26(2): 168–189. (Denny and Spirling 2018)
Read this alongside our cleaning steps. The authors show that preprocessing choices, including stemming, stopwords, and lowercasing, can change substantive conclusions, and that their order matters. Their analysis concerns unsupervised learning, but supervised pipelines also need scrutiny beyond an accuracy score.
Barberá, P., Boydstun, A. E., Linn, S., McMahon, R., and Nagler, J. 2021. “Automated Text Classification of News Articles: A Practical Guide to Using Supervised Machine Learning Methods.” Political Analysis 29(1): 19–42. (Barberá et al. 2021)
This is a practical companion to our exercise. Focus on the human coding stage, especially the number of coders and how to handle disagreement. Our corpus has only one coder, which limits what we can establish about the labels.
Recommended, not required.
Hopkins, D. J., and King, G. 2010. “A Method of Automated Nonparametric Content Analysis for Social Science.” American Journal of Political Science 54(1): 229–247. (Hopkins and King 2010)
Read this if your project will estimate category proportions rather than retrieve individual documents. The authors show why optimizing document-level accuracy can still produce biased proportions when errors do not cancel. That distinction matters for questions such as the share of tweets concerning immigration.

4.8 Questions for the session
Prepare an answer to at least two questions.

The independence assumption is false of language and the classifier works anyway. What does that suggest about the relationship between the realism of a model’s assumptions and its usefulness? Is your answer the same for a predictive model as for an explanatory one?
Our cleaning pipeline deleted @ThomasHomanICE, the handle of the acting director of ICE, whose presence is close to decisive evidence about a tweet’s topic. Defend the deletion. Then defend the opposite choice. Which argument would you actually make in a paper, and what would you have to report either way?
The coding scheme decides that immigration mentioned as the seventh item in a list of accomplishments is other. A different coder could decide otherwise. Trace what would change: the labels, the model, the accuracy, and the substantive claim you would end up making about how much of Trump’s 2019 output concerned immigration.
The classes were deliberately made roughly balanced, which makes accuracy more interpretable but means the corpus does not represent the full tweet stream. What would you change if your question concerned the share of Trump’s 2019 tweets about immigration rather than the classification of individual tweets?
This handout built a machine that reads political speech and decides what it is about, using roughly forty lines of R and 724 labeled examples. Given how little that took, what follows about who is able to build such systems, and about what a political scientist’s distinctive contribution to them should be?

title: 5  Large Language Models
text:
5.1 Part I. Categories you did not supply
Week 5, 30 September
Over the last three weeks, we have used supervised methods to predict outcomes from labeled cases. We chose categories, supplied examples, and evaluated predictions on cases excluded from fitting. Neighbors, trees, and word rates implemented this in different ways.
This week we explore two alternatives.
First, we try an unsupervised model. If we do not know which distinctions to look for in a corpus, we can ask a model to find structure, then assess whether its groupings are useful. We still have to interpret and name them, so this changes where the coding decisions occur.
Second, we use a large language model. We can describe categories in English and ask it to apply them without fitting it to our own labeled training data. We will examine both the convenience of this approach and its limitations.

title: 5  Large Language Models
text:
5.1.1 Supervised and unsupervised
Our methods so far have been supervised: each training case had a known outcome. The model learned to reproduce those outcomes, and we evaluated it by comparing its predictions with held-out labels.
Unsupervised methods look for structure without supplied outcomes. They may identify similar documents or words that often occur together. There are no correct labels against which to calculate the same kind of accuracy score, so we need other ways to evaluate the result.
A common approach in political text analysis is topic modeling, particularly Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA). It represents each document as a mixture of topics and each topic as a distribution over words. Fitting estimates both distributions together.
An unsupervised model can return plausible-looking output even when it is unhelpful. We begin with an example of that problem.


5.1.2 The corpus, and a subset of it

install.packages(c("tm", "SnowballC", "topicmodels", "slam", "ggplot2"))


library(tm)
library(SnowballC)
library(topicmodels)
library(slam)
library(ggplot2)

url <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/babakrezaee/",
              "AppliedAI-PoliSci/refs/heads/main/data/",
              "trump_2019_all.csv")

all <- read.csv(url, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, na.strings = "")

nrow(all)

[1] 4148

table(all$label, useNA = "ifany")


immigration       other        <NA> 
        367         538        3243 


This corpus contains every original tweet from 2019 after removing retweets, link-only tweets, and duplicates. Last week’s 905 tweets are a subset, marked by the label column. The other three thousand have no hand labels.
We use the same cleaning pipeline as Week 4.

corpus <- VCorpus(VectorSource(all$text))

replace_with_space <- content_transformer(function(x, pattern) {
  gsub(pattern, " ", x)
})

clean <- tm_map(corpus, content_transformer(tolower))
clean <- tm_map(clean, replace_with_space, "http[s]?://\\S*")
clean <- tm_map(clean, replace_with_space, "@\\S+")
clean <- tm_map(clean, replace_with_space, "[^a-z ]")
clean <- tm_map(clean, removeWords, stopwords("english"))
clean <- tm_map(clean, stemDocument)
clean <- tm_map(clean, stripWhitespace)

dtm <- DocumentTermMatrix(clean)

dtm

<<DocumentTermMatrix (documents: 4148, terms: 5455)>>
Non-/sparse entries: 67963/22559377
Sparsity           : 100%
Maximal term length: 28
Weighting          : term frequency (tf)


Some tweets contain almost nothing beyond links and handles. Cleaning leaves them with no words, producing zero rows. LDA() cannot fit those rows, so we remove them first.

keep <- row_sums(dtm) > 0

sum(!keep)

[1] 3

First, fit the model to the familiar subset of 905 hand-labeled tweets.

wk4 <- which(!is.na(all$label) & keep)

length(wk4)

[1] 905

lda_wk4 <- LDA(dtm[wk4, ], k = 6, control = list(seed = 7))

terms(lda_wk4, 10)

 [2,] "now"      "great"    "wall"   "border"   "will"       "illeg"

[10,] "southern" "get"      "much"   "secur"    "presid"     "republican"


Look at the six columns and try to name the topics before reading further.
Naming them is difficult. Every column contains border or wall, along with words such as will, great, democrat, and presid. The six topics look very similar. The model ran without a warning and returned the expected format, but the result is not useful for separating subjects.


5.1.4 Why, and what that tells you
To understand this result, look at how the corpus was assembled.

probe <- as.matrix(dtm[, c("border", "wall", "mexico")]) > 0

round(100 * colMeans(probe[wk4, ]), 1)

border   wall mexico 
  32.3   15.9   10.7 

round(100 * colMeans(probe[keep, ]), 1)

border   wall mexico 
   7.0    3.5    2.3 


border occurs in roughly three of every ten tweets in the Week 4 corpus, compared with fewer than one in ten across the full year. We included all immigration tweets and deliberately chose negative examples containing near misses such as border, wall, and illegal. That construction made a useful Naive Bayes exercise, but gives the topic model little topical diversity to separate.
The corpus shapes an unsupervised result as much as the method does. Supervised evaluation can reveal poor performance against labels. Here we receive six well-formatted columns and have to assess their usefulness ourselves. Readers also need enough information about the corpus to make that assessment.


5.1.5 The same model, the whole year

lda_all <- LDA(dtm[keep, ], k = 6, control = list(seed = 7))

terms(lda_all, 10)

      Topic 1 Topic 2    Topic 3  Topic 4    Topic 5      Topic 6     
 [1,] "will"  "democrat" "presid" "will"     "great"      "great"     
 [2,] "now"   "great"    "state"  "democrat" "will"       "just"      
 [3,] "peopl" "year"     "time"   "countri"  "now"        "american"

[10,] "look"  "state"    "like"   "china"    "get"        "democrat"  


The full-year topics differ more clearly. Alongside the border debate, this corpus contains impeachment, the Mueller report, trade with China, the economy, rallies, and endorsements.


5.1.6 Reading the model properly
terms() is a convenient summary. The estimates themselves are in two matrices. We will extract them because they supply the quantities for the following figures.

post <- posterior(lda_all)

beta <- post$terms     # 6 topics by vocabulary: word probabilities within a topic
gamma <- post$topics   # documents by 6 topics: topic shares within a document

dim(beta)

[1]    6 5455

dim(gamma)

[1] 4145    6




5.1.7 The top words in each topic

top <- data.frame()

for (k in 1:6) {
  o <- order(beta[k, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:10]
  top <- rbind(top, data.frame(topic = k,
                               term  = colnames(beta)[o],
                               beta  = beta[k, o]))
}

top$lab <- factor(paste(top$topic, top$term),
                  levels = rev(paste(top$topic, top$term)))

ggplot(top, aes(beta, lab)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ topic, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) sub("^[0-9]+ ", "", x)) +
  labs(x = "probability of the word within the topic", y = NULL,
       title = "Most probable words in each topic")








This plot adds probabilities to the top words printed by terms(). The steep drop in bar height shows that two or three words carry much of each displayed topic’s probability, while the remaining top words contribute less.


5.1.8 The words that actually separate the topics
The most probable words are not always the most useful for distinguishing topics. Words such as will and great are common across the corpus and appear near the top of several topics.
Instead, ask which words are more likely in a topic than in the corpus overall.

p_corpus <- col_sums(dtm[keep, ])
p_corpus <- p_corpus / sum(p_corpus)
p_corpus <- p_corpus[colnames(beta)]

lift <- sweep(log2(beta), 2, log2(p_corpus), "-")

lift[beta < 0.0015] <- NA   # ignore words too rare to be worth reporting

dist <- data.frame()

for (k in 1:6) {
  o <- order(lift[k, ], decreasing = TRUE, na.last = NA)[1:10]
  dist <- rbind(dist, data.frame(topic = k,
                                 term  = colnames(lift)[o],
                                 lift  = lift[k, o]))
}

dist$lab <- factor(paste(dist$topic, dist$term),
                   levels = rev(paste(dist$topic, dist$term)))

ggplot(dist, aes(lift, lab)) +
  geom_col(fill = "maroon") +
  facet_wrap(~ topic, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) sub("^[0-9]+ ", "", x)) +
  labs(x = "log2 times more likely in this topic than in the corpus", y = NULL,
       title = "Most distinctive words in each topic")








A value of 2 means a word is four times more likely in the topic than in the whole corpus. This comparison reduces the prominence of shared vocabulary and highlights differences.
There are two cautions. I chose the threshold 0.0015 to exclude very rare words with high lift; it is arbitrary, so try changing it. Also, distinctiveness and importance are different properties. Read this plot alongside the probability plot.






Tip



Try the distinctiveness plot on lda_wk4. The short bars and similar words across panels make its limited separation easier to see than the printed table does.




5.1.9 Documents are mixtures, not members
LDA has not assigned each tweet to one box. Each tweet has a share of every topic, and those shares sum to one.

gdf <- data.frame(topic = factor(rep(1:6, each = nrow(gamma))),
                  gamma = as.vector(gamma))

ggplot(gdf, aes(topic, gamma)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey90", outlier.size = 0.4, outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "topic", y = "share of a document belonging to this topic",
       title = "How much of each document belongs to each topic")








The long upper tails suggest that many tweets are dominated by one topic, while others have substantial shares of several. Unlike Naive Bayes’s single label or a tree’s single path, this allows a tweet to be sixty percent one topic and forty percent another. Such mixtures can better describe political text, though they are harder to summarize in a simple table.


5.1.10 Against the hand labels
We have human labels for 905 tweets, so we can compare the topic structure with a category defined by a coder. Many topic-model applications lack this comparison.

lab <- all$label[keep]
assigned <- topics(lda_all)

tab <- table(topic = assigned[!is.na(lab)], label = lab[!is.na(lab)])

hdf <- as.data.frame(prop.table(tab, 2))

ggplot(hdf, aes(label, topic, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * Freq)), size = 3.4) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "topic", fill = "share of\ncolumn",
       title = "Where the hand-coded tweets land")








Read the figure by column. Immigration tweets concentrate in one or two topics, but those topics also contain tweets labeled other.
The labels and topics are related but answer different questions. The coder decided whether immigration was a main subject of each tweet. LDA estimated patterns of word co-occurrence across the corpus. We should not expect the two to coincide exactly.


5.1.11 Naming, and what naming costs
The figures do not supply topic names. LDA returns numbered word distributions; calling topic 3 “immigration” requires our interpretation of the words.
Unsupervised learning therefore moves some coding decisions to after the analysis. We should report those decisions clearly, since a topic name can otherwise look like something the model discovered on its own.
Two other choices remain ours. I set k to six; the data did not determine that value. With twenty topics, the border, caravan, and wall might appear separately rather than together. Cleaning also matters because stemming and stopwords determine which words are available to define the topics.
Topic models are useful for exploring a corpus we have not read in full. Their topics are not automatically measurements of a predefined concept. Treating them that way requires further justification and validation.

title: 5  Large Language Models
section: 5.2 Part II. What a language model is
text:
5.2 Part II. What a language model is
Before calling a language model, we need a basic account of how it works. We will leave the mathematics aside and focus on ideas that help explain its behavior in the exercise.

5.2.1 One operation, repeated
A language model assigns probabilities to possible next pieces of text given the preceding text. A selection process chooses one, and the operation repeats.

The figure introduces four terms we will use.
A token is a unit of text, often part of a word. For example, willing may be split into will and ing, while an unusual name may take several tokens. Token counts also determine billing.
An embedding represents a token as a vector. Similar uses of words can produce similar vectors, helping the model relate protest to demonstration. The intuition resembles Week 2’s distances, but these coordinates are learned rather than measured directly.
Attention lets a token’s representation incorporate the surrounding tokens. This helps distinguish bank in a river sentence from bank in a financial sentence. It is a central architectural feature of these models.
The context window is the amount of text the model can work with at once, including prompt and answer. Text outside that window is unavailable for the current response.
Classification, summarization, translation, and code generation use this same repeated operation under different prompts. When we request a sentiment label, the model generates a continuation consistent with that request rather than consulting a separate sentiment module.


5.2.2 Where it came from
The model has already undergone training before it answers our call. Two stages are useful to distinguish.

During pre-training, the model repeatedly predicts the next token in a large volume of text. Backpropagation calculates how its weights contributed to the error and adjusts them to reduce it. Through this process, the model acquires patterns of grammar, facts, and style. It also reflects the distribution of its training material, including which voices are common and which are scarce.
The resulting base model predicts plausible continuations but is not yet shaped for assistant-style conversation. For example, it may continue a question with another question instead of answering it.
Post-training shapes that behavior. Instruction tuning uses instructions paired with suitable responses. Preference tuning uses judgments about which of several responses is better. This helps make the model an assistant, while incorporating decisions about what counts as a good, safe, or appropriate answer. Both training stages influence judgments such as calling a tweet “critical” or “diplomatic.”


5.2.3 Nothing you do changes it
During our calls, the model’s weights are fixed. It reads the prompt and generates an answer without updating those weights.
Few-shot examples therefore do not train the model in the sense of changing its parameters. They give it context for the current task. Think of supplying instructions and examples for someone to consult while answering.
Our data are not used to fit the model during the call, but they are transmitted to the provider. How they are processed is a separate question governed by the provider’s terms. The owner can also replace the model version, making API-based measurements dependent on the service available at the time.

title: 5  Large Language Models
section: 5.3 Part III. Talking to a model from R
text:
5.3 Part III. Talking to a model from R

5.3.1 What is actually happening
The model runs on the company’s hardware, not your laptop. R sends text over the internet and receives a response through an API, an interface through which programs communicate.
This has practical implications. Calls cost money and need a network connection. They also send data to another organization’s system, which matters much more for interview transcripts than for public tweets. Finally, the service owner can change the model we access.


5.3.2 The key, and where it does not go
An API key identifies the account used for access and billing. You have each been issued one for this course.
Keep the key out of scripts, including comments and temporary test code. Scripts can end up in repositories, and exposed keys can be found and used by others. Charges go to the account owner.
Store the key in an environment variable outside the project. ellmer reads it automatically, so it does not need to appear in the analysis code.

usethis::edit_r_environ()

This opens .Renviron. Add a line with no quotation marks or spaces around the equals sign:
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-your-key-here
Save the file and restart R, since it reads .Renviron at startup. Check that the key is available without printing it:

nchar(Sys.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY")) > 0

TRUE means the key is available. If you see FALSE, check that you saved the file and restarted R.






Important



Treat the key like a password. Do not paste it into Brightspace, messages, or chat windows. If you think it has been exposed, tell me so I can revoke it. All course keys will be revoked at the end of the block.




5.3.3 The first call

install.packages("ellmer")


library(ellmer)

model_name <- "gpt-5.6-luna"

chat <- chat_openai(model = model_name, echo = "none")

chat$chat("In a few short sentences, tell me about Leiden University.")

chat_openai() creates a chat object, and model selects the model. Setting echo = "none" returns the answer as a value rather than streaming it to the console, which is useful when storing output in an object.
ellmer handles the request, authentication, and response parsing. It also supports Anthropic through chat_anthropic() and Google through chat_google_gemini(). This gives us a similar interface across providers and makes it easier to change services later.
The chat object is stateful: it retains the conversation and includes earlier exchanges when we ask follow-up questions.

chat$chat("Which faculty is it best known for?")

That is useful for conversation, but can complicate classification. Reusing one conversation for five hundred tweets means later tweets are judged with earlier ones in context. For independent classification, each document should be processed separately, as in the next section.

title: 5  Large Language Models
section: 5.4 Part IV. One call becomes a column
text:
5.4 Part IV. One call becomes a column
We now return to text classification using NATO tweets. We will ask the model to label each tweet’s sentiment and tone.

nato <- read.csv(paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/babakrezaee/",
                        "MethodsCourses/refs/heads/master/DataSets/",
                        "nato_tweets.csv"),
                 stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

nrow(nato)

head(nato$tweet_text, 3)


5.4.1 The obvious approach, and why we are not using it
One approach is to ask in plain English and then extract the answer.

chat$chat(paste(
  "Classify the sentiment of this tweet as positive, negative, or neutral.",
  "Reply in the format 'Sentiment: [sentiment]'.",
  nato$tweet_text[1]
))

This often works for a few cases, but becomes fragile at scale. The model might return “cautiously optimistic” instead of one sentiment word, add a preamble, or vary capitalization. A parser may then return missing values or treat equivalent responses as separate categories.
These problems may go unnoticed in a large output column. Parsing free text needs careful checks, because format variations can become missing values or incorrect category counts without stopping the analysis.


5.4.2 Declaring the shape of the answer
An alternative is to specify the output structure before making the request. In ellmer, we declare a type.

type_tweet <- type_object(
  "Sentiment and tone of a political tweet.",
  sentiment = type_enum(
    c("positive", "negative", "neutral"),
    "Overall sentiment of the tweet."
  ),
  tone = type_enum(
    c("formal", "urgent", "diplomatic", "critical", "neutral"),
    "Dominant tone of the tweet."
  )
)

type_object() defines named fields, and type_enum() restricts a field to listed values. Their descriptions are sent to the model as instructions. They are part of the prompt, so write them as carefully as a codebook definition.
For one tweet:

chat$chat_structured(nato$tweet_text[1], type = type_tweet)

For the full set, parallel_chat_structured() sends requests concurrently and returns one row per input:

results <- parallel_chat_structured(
  chat,
  as.list(nato$tweet_text),
  type = type_tweet
)

nato$sentiment <- results$sentiment
nato$tone      <- results$tone

head(nato[, c("tweet_text", "sentiment", "tone")])

table(nato$sentiment)

The package handles requests and structured responses, so we do not need our own POST calls, nested-list parsing, regular expressions, loops, progress bars, or preallocated matrices. This reduces the amount of code needed and avoids several opportunities for unnoticed format errors.
With type_enum(), the permitted categories are known before the run. Week 4 restricted predictions through the training labels; here we restrict them through a declaration in the script. Both keep the category set consistent, though a correctly shaped response still needs substantive validation.


5.4.3 Showing it one or two examples
We have described the categories but supplied no examples of applying them. We can add a few already-coded cases to clarify our intended meaning, without building a conventional labeled training set.
One example is one-shot prompting; several make it few-shot. The examples become part of the prompt. They do not fit new parameters, but provide additional context for interpreting the instruction.
Here we place the examples in the system prompt, the first argument to chat_openai(), which accompanies each request.

instructions <- "
You are coding tweets from official NATO and allied government accounts
for a political science project.

Code the overall sentiment and the dominant tone of each tweet.

Two examples of how this codebook is applied:

Tweet: 'Allied forces completed the exercise successfully. We thank our
partners in the region for their professionalism and cooperation.'
sentiment: positive
tone: formal

Tweet: 'Russia's continued strikes on civilian infrastructure are
unacceptable and must stop immediately.'
sentiment: negative
tone: critical

Note that a tweet may report a difficult situation in measured language.
Code the sentiment of the situation described, not the politeness of the
wording.
"

chat_few <- chat_openai(instructions, model = model_name, echo = "none")

results_few <- parallel_chat_structured(
  chat_few,
  as.list(nato$tweet_text),
  type = type_tweet
)

nato$sentiment_few <- results_few$sentiment
nato$tone_few      <- results_few$tone

The prompt’s final sentence clarifies an ambiguity in diplomatic language that the examples alone may not settle. Examples demonstrate a rule; explicit instructions state it. Using both resembles writing a codebook with definitions and worked cases.


5.4.4 Did it change anything?
Without human labels for these tweets, we cannot compare accuracy. We can, however, measure how much the outputs change between prompts.

table(zero_shot = nato$sentiment, few_shot = nato$sentiment_few)

mean(nato$sentiment != nato$sentiment_few)

The off-diagonal cells count tweets given different labels after the prompt changed. The text stayed the same, but the measurement changed.
Compare this with Week 4. Its fitted classifier returns a fixed label for a given tweet unless we change the data or model. Here, two reasonable prompts produce different labels from identical text. Looking at one run alone would not reveal that sensitivity.
Reporting the prompt is useful, but it does not show whether a finding depends on its wording. The disagreement rate gives us a simple additional check to report.
Keep two things in mind when using examples.
Keep examples separate from evaluation cases. If a few-shot example comes from the test set, the model has seen part of the answer before evaluation. This is the same type of information leakage we guarded against when selecting Week 4’s vocabulary. Hold those examples out.
More examples may not improve the result. They increase the tokens used in every call, and an unrepresentative set can encourage an unsuitable rule. Ornstein and colleagues examine when few-shot prompting helps. Read their findings for those conditions rather than as advice to keep adding examples.

write.csv(nato, "nato_tweets_scored.csv", row.names = FALSE)

section: 5.5 Part V. What kind of model is this?
text:
5.5 Part V. What kind of model is this?
Before moving on, compare this setup with the models we fitted in earlier weeks.
We did not fit a model to this corpus. There is no training/test split or parameter estimated from these tweets. We began with zero-shot classification and then supplied two examples in the prompt. Those examples add guidance without updating the model’s weights. This reduces our labeling work from hundreds of documents to a few or none.
We cannot inspect a fitted object in the same way. Week 4 exposed word-rate tables, and today’s topic model gave us two matrices. The commercial language model provides no comparable object to examine. Its many parameters are inaccessible and would be difficult to interpret even with access.
Repeated results are not guaranteed to match. Sampling can change the answer to the same tweet. Prompt changes can alter labels too, and the owner may replace or withdraw the model. Once a version is unavailable, exact reruns may be impossible. Locally fitted models are easier to preserve, subject to maintaining the software needed to run them.
There is a per-document charge. This affects the scale and design of a study, unlike applying a locally fitted classifier without API fees.

title: 5  Large Language Models
text:
5.6 What we have not done
So far, we have produced labels without checking whether they are correct.
The NATO tweets have no human labels to compare with the output. We therefore have a sentiment column without evidence of its accuracy. If we stopped here, we could only say that a commercial model assigned those values, not that they are valid measurements.
Week 6 addresses evaluation. We will use a corpus with human labels, like the one from Week 4, to examine the model’s classifications.
For now, the exercise shows that an LLM can return structured classifications quickly and cheaply without our own labeled training set. It has not shown that those classifications are accurate.

title: 5  Large Language Models
section: 5.7 The politics of a rented classifier
text:
5.7 The politics of a rented classifier
After similarity, thresholds, and codebooks, another issue arises: who controls the classifier?
We access this classifier as a service. We cannot inspect its weights, preserve the deployed version, or prevent its owner from changing or withdrawing it. This complicates research replication when published measurements depend on a model version that later becomes unavailable.
Its judgments also reflect the text used in training, including the prominence of internet material and English. Deciding between “critical” and “diplomatic” draws on learned language patterns. For comparisons across countries or languages, we would want to know whose speech is well represented. From outside the provider, that is difficult to establish.
Access depends on resources. This exercise is possible because the course has a budget for calls. Researchers without funding, or in countries where a service is unavailable, may not be able to use the same method. Those differences can shape which questions get studied and by whom.
These considerations do not rule out using LLMs. They help us explain the conditions and limitations of the measurements we make with them.

5.8 Reading
Ornstein, J. T., Blasingame, E. N., and Truscott, J. S. 2025. “How to Train Your Stochastic Parrot: Large Language Models for Political Texts.” Political Science Research and Methods. (Ornstein et al. 2025)
This article offers practical guidance for political scientists and reports preregistered tests. Few-shot prompting matches or outperforms conventional supervised classifiers across its sentiment, scaling, and topic tasks without preprocessing or a conventional labeled training set. Compare it with Week 4, focusing on the conditions under which prompting can replace that pipeline.
Gilardi, F., Alizadeh, M., and Kubli, M. 2023. “ChatGPT Outperforms Crowd Workers for Text-Annotation Tasks.” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 120(30): e2305016120. (Gilardi et al. 2023)
Pay attention to the comparison behind the headline. The benchmark is crowd workers, rather than expert coders using a developed codebook, and the tasks have relatively clear boundaries. Consider how the result might differ for our more contested coding rules.
Grimmer, J., and Stewart, B. M. 2013. “Text as Data: The Promise and Pitfalls of Automatic Content Analysis Methods for Political Texts.” Political Analysis 21(3): 267–297. (Grimmer and Stewart 2013)
Return to the sections on unsupervised methods. Their account of topic-model validation and interpretation is useful for assessing our topic names and the heatmap comparing topics with human labels.

text:
5.10 Questions for the session
Prepare an answer to at least two questions.

LDA returned six numbered distributions over words, and a researcher named them. Week 4 began with a codebook written before any data was read. Both are acts of category creation by a human being. Which is more defensible, and which is more likely to be reported honestly in a published article?
The zero-shot run classified five hundred tweets without being shown a single labeled example. What, exactly, is it using in place of the training data, and what would you need to know about that in order to trust the result?
Run the same tweet through the model twice and you may get two different answers, and change the prompt and a share of the corpus is measured differently. State what those two facts together do to the replication standards you have been taught elsewhere in this program, and what a defensible reporting practice would look like.
This week’s method requires a budget; Week 4’s required a person willing to read nine hundred tweets. Both are costs, and they fall on different people. Which of the two is more likely to determine what gets studied, and by whom?
You now have two ways to measure whether a tweet is about immigration: train a classifier on hand labels, or ask a language model in English. Suppose the two disagree about a hundred tweets. Describe how you would decide which is right, and notice that your answer is the subject of Week 6.
Adding two examples and one clarifying sentence to the prompt changed the coding of some tweets, and we have no way of knowing which version is closer to the truth. Is the few-shot version better, and on what grounds would you defend your answer to a reviewer?

title: 6  Evaluating AI Systems
text:
6.1 Part I. What accuracy hides
Week 6, 7 October
Last week, we classified NATO tweets with a language model but had no human labels to check its answers. We have now applied it to the 181 tweets in Week 4’s test set, where we do have hand-coded labels. The language model received instructions but no labeled examples.
It agrees with the human coder on 95 percent of those tweets. The Naive Bayes model, trained on 724 hand-coded tweets, reaches roughly 90 percent. On those figures alone, prompting a language model looks like an easier and better option. What else do we need to know before drawing that conclusion?
Both scores are accurate for this comparison. This session examines what they measure and which conclusions they support.
We focus on two issues. First, agreement with a coder and codebook is not automatically correspondence with the concept we want to measure. Second, labels that are 95 percent correct need not produce estimates that are 95 percent correct. Systematic labeling errors can bias the analysis that uses them.

title: 6  Evaluating AI Systems
text:
6.1.1 The classifier, rebuilt
Part I reuses the Week 4 pipeline in a compressed form. Refer back to that handout for explanations of its individual steps.

install.packages(c("tm", "SnowballC", "caret", "e1071", "ggplot2", "pROC"))


library(tm)
library(SnowballC)
library(caret)
library(ggplot2)

url4 <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/babakrezaee/",
               "AppliedAI-PoliSci/refs/heads/main/data/",
               "trump_immigration_2019.csv")

tweets <- read.csv(url4, stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
                   colClasses = c(id = "character"))
tweets$label <- factor(tweets$label, levels = c("other", "immigration"))

corpus <- VCorpus(VectorSource(tweets$text))

replace_with_space <- content_transformer(function(x, pattern) {
  gsub(pattern, " ", x)
})

clean <- tm_map(corpus, content_transformer(tolower))
clean <- tm_map(clean, replace_with_space, "http[s]?://\\S*")
clean <- tm_map(clean, replace_with_space, "@\\S+")
clean <- tm_map(clean, replace_with_space, "[^a-z ]")
clean <- tm_map(clean, removeWords, stopwords("english"))
clean <- tm_map(clean, stemDocument)
clean <- tm_map(clean, stripWhitespace)

dtm <- DocumentTermMatrix(clean)

train_id <- 1:floor(0.8 * nrow(tweets))

freq_words <- findFreqTerms(dtm[train_id, ], 5)

counts_train <- as.matrix(dtm[train_id, freq_words])
counts_test  <- as.matrix(dtm[-train_id, freq_words])

y_train <- tweets$label[train_id]
y_test  <- tweets$label[-train_id]

total_immigration <- colSums(counts_train[y_train == "immigration", ])
total_other       <- colSums(counts_train[y_train == "other", ])

p_immigration <- (total_immigration + 1) / sum(total_immigration + 1)
p_other       <- (total_other + 1) / sum(total_other + 1)

# The two scores, exactly as in Week 4
score_immigration <- as.vector(counts_test %*% log(p_immigration)) +
  log(mean(y_train == "immigration"))

score_other <- as.vector(counts_test %*% log(p_other)) +
  log(mean(y_train == "other"))

# Week 4 classified by asking which score was larger. The same comparison,
# written as a probability that the tweet is about immigration:
prob <- 1 / (1 + exp(-(score_immigration - score_other)))

nb_pred <- factor(ifelse(prob > 0.5, "immigration", "other"),
                  levels = c("other", "immigration"))

The following line adds the quantity we need for this part.
Week 4 compared score_immigration with score_other. These are sums of logarithms, and neither score is directly interpretable on its own. The new line converts their difference into \(P(\text{immigration} \mid \text{tweet})\), the classifier’s assigned probability. The logistic transformation preserves the ranking of tweets.
The default threshold is 0.5. Above it, the model predicts immigration. This is equivalent to choosing the class with the higher score. We will now examine what changes when we move that threshold.


6.1.2 Precision and recall, at last
Precision and recall describe different aspects of the same confusion matrix. Both depend on which class we designate as positive.

cm <- confusionMatrix(nb_pred, y_test, positive = "immigration")

cm$table

             Reference
Prediction    other immigration
  other          82           5
  immigration    12          82

round(cm$byClass[c("Precision", "Recall", "F1")], 3)

Precision    Recall        F1 
    0.872     0.943     0.906 


Using TP, FP, FN, and TN for its cells, with immigration as the positive class:
\[
\text{Recall} = \text{Sensitivity} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}
\qquad
\text{Specificity} = \frac{TN}{TN + FP}
\]
\[
\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}
\qquad
F_1 = 2 \cdot \frac{\text{Recall} \times \text{Precision}}{\text{Recall} + \text{Precision}}
\]
The denominators explain the difference. Recall, also called sensitivity or the true positive rate, divides by all genuine immigration tweets: what share did the model find? Precision, or positive predictive value, divides by all tweets the model flagged: what share were genuinely about immigration? A classifier can find most relevant cases while also producing many false alarms.
Specificity measures the share of genuine negatives correctly identified. It matters when avoiding errors on that class is important. \(F_1\) combines precision and recall through their harmonic mean, so a low value on either pulls the combined score down.
The mode argument tells caret which set of measures to report:

confusionMatrix(nb_pred, y_test, positive = "immigration",
                mode = "prec_recall")$byClass[c("Precision", "Recall", "F1")]

Precision    Recall        F1 
0.8723404 0.9425287 0.9060773 

confusionMatrix(nb_pred, y_test, positive = "immigration",
                mode = "sens_spec")$byClass[c("Sensitivity", "Specificity")]

Sensitivity Specificity 
  0.9425287   0.8723404 


Precision and recall also depend on the threshold used to turn scores into labels. We can see that by moving the cut point.


6.1.3 The threshold is a choice, not a finding
The 0.5 threshold is a convention. Changing it gives different classifications from the same fitted model. The appropriate cut point depends on the task, rather than being determined by the data alone.

cuts <- seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.1)

sweep_out <- data.frame()

for (cc in cuts) {
  pred_c <- factor(ifelse(prob > cc, "immigration", "other"),
                   levels = c("other", "immigration"))
  tp <- sum(pred_c == "immigration" & y_test == "immigration")
  fp <- sum(pred_c == "immigration" & y_test == "other")
  fn <- sum(pred_c == "other" & y_test == "immigration")
  tn <- sum(pred_c == "other" & y_test == "other")
  sweep_out <- rbind(sweep_out,
                     data.frame(threshold = cc,
                                flagged   = tp + fp,
                                precision = tp / (tp + fp),
                                recall    = tp / (tp + fn),
                                accuracy  = (tp + tn) / length(y_test)))
}

sweep_out$default <- sweep_out$threshold == 0.5

round(sweep_out[, 1:5], 3)

  threshold flagged precision recall accuracy
1       0.1     106     0.802  0.977    0.873
2       0.2     100     0.840  0.966    0.895
3       0.3      99     0.848  0.966    0.901
4       0.4      96     0.865  0.954    0.906
5       0.5      94     0.872  0.943    0.906

Each row summarizes a confusion matrix at a different threshold. At 0.1, the classifier finds nearly all immigration tweets but also flags many others. At 0.9, its flagged tweets are mostly correct, but it misses more genuine cases. The marked 0.5 row is the default, not necessarily the best choice for our purpose.

ggplot(sweep_out, aes(recall, precision)) +
  geom_path(colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey25", size = 1.9) +
  geom_text(aes(label = threshold), size = 3.1, colour = "grey25",
            hjust = -0.35, vjust = -0.5) +
  geom_point(data = sweep_out[sweep_out$default, ],
             colour = "maroon", size = 3.4) +
  geom_text(data = sweep_out[sweep_out$default, ],
            label = "default, p = 0.5", colour = "maroon",
            size = 3.3, hjust = 1.15, vjust = 1.8) +
  expand_limits(x = max(sweep_out$recall) + 0.04) +
  labs(x = "recall", y = "precision",
       title = "Every point is the same classifier, cut in a different place",
       subtitle = "Labels are the probability threshold for flagging a tweet")








The plot shows this trade-off. Each label marks a threshold and its precision and recall. The maroon point is the default; nearby points show what happens if we change it.


6.1.4 Why there is a trade-off at all
To understand the trade-off, look at how the two denominators behave as we lower the threshold.
One denominator stays fixed; the other changes with the classifier’s decisions.
Recall divides by the 87 genuine immigration tweets in the test set. Lowering the threshold catches more of them, so recall rises. Precision divides by the number flagged, which grows as we lower the threshold. The additional tweets have weaker scores and include more false positives, so precision falls in this example.
As a practical guide, precision emphasizes confidence in a flag; recall emphasizes finding the relevant cases.
Think about a spam filter. Letting a spam message into your inbox is usually a nuisance, while hiding a genuine job offer or exam result in junk may be costly. That makes precision important: when the filter labels a message as spam, we want it to be right, even if some spam gets through.
For a screening test for a serious disease, missing a case may be more costly than arranging an additional test after a false alarm. That favors recall, with further checks used to investigate flagged cases. The mathematics is the same, but the costs point toward a different threshold.
For our classifier, the appropriate balance depends on how we plan to use the labels. The default 0.5 does not settle that decision.


6.1.5 Try it yourself
Move the threshold and watch the four cells change. The display uses the same 181 test tweets as the table above. It follows caret’s layout: predictions down the side and reference labels across the top.

data = transpose(eval_data)







viewof t = Inputs.range([0.01, 0.99], {value: 0.5, step: 0.01,
  label: "Flag a tweet when the probability exceeds"})







counts = {
  let tp = 0, fp = 0, fn = 0, tn = 0;
  for (const d of data) {
    const flagged = d.prob > t;
    const positive = d.truth === "immigration";
    if (flagged && positive) tp++;
    else if (flagged && !positive) fp++;
    else if (!flagged && positive) fn++;
    else tn++;
  }
  return {tp: tp, fp: fp, fn: fn, tn: tn};
}

curve = {
  const out = [];
  for (let c = 0.01; c <= 0.99; c += 0.01) {
    let tp = 0, fp = 0, fn = 0;
    for (const d of data) {
      const f = d.prob > c, p = d.truth === "immigration";
      if (f && p) tp++; else if (f && !p) fp++; else if (!f && p) fn++;
    }
    if (tp + fp > 0) out.push({recall: tp / (tp + fn), precision: tp / (tp + fp)});
  }

Plot.plot({
  width: 560, height: 380, marginLeft: 55, marginBottom: 45,
  x: {label: "recall", domain: [0, 1]},
  y: {label: "precision", domain: [0, 1]},

    Plot.dot([{recall: counts.tp / (counts.tp + counts.fn),
